FODO.summary:
In January 1862 a Union reconnaissance concluded that the weakest points in the Confederacy’s western defense line were two earthen forts guarding the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers. On February 6 Flag Officer Andrew Foote’s gunboats pounded Fort Henry into submission; almost 2,500 of its garrison escaped a dozen miles to Fort Donelson, on the Cumberland near Dover, Tennessee. There, on February 14, the Confederate river batteries drove off Foote’s ironclads in a 90-minute duel. A Confederate breakout the next day briefly opened an escape route before confused commanders ordered their men back to the trenches, and on February 16 Brigadier General Ulysses S. Grant answered a request for terms: no terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender. An estimated 13,000 Confederate soldiers were shipped north to prison camps. [1]

It was the North’s first major victory of the war. The South gave up southern Kentucky and much of Middle and West Tennessee, and the rivers became Union supply lines into the Confederate heartland. The park’s foundation document adds that the campaign saw the war’s first use of inland ironclad gunboats and its first joint Army–Navy operation, and that the Union presence drew enslaved people to seek freedom, leading to Free State, which it calls one of the first freedmen’s communities in Tennessee, and perhaps the nation. Fort Donelson became a national military park on March 26, 1928, and a national battlefield on August 16, 1985. [1] [1]

black.html: After the surrender, enslaved people from nearby plantations came into the Union lines. Ten days after it, Grant issued General Orders No. 14, which barred slaveholders from his lines; he would not return people to their enslavers, and he sought government work for those who had built the Confederate fort. Freedom seekers kept coming. Their settlement southwest of the Union fort became known as Free State, probably one and the same as the army’s contraband camp, whose men built the new Union Fort Donelson in 1863 and enlisted as United States Colored Troops; teachers from Indiana opened a school there in March 1864 that by May had 100 pupils. The brochure says an estimated 300 enslaved people wintered at Fort Donelson in 1864; the study quotes an 1867 description of Free State as numbering about 300. Free State lasted for decades and became an African American neighborhood of Dover. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Fort Donelson NB archive page — overview (from the NPS brochure) and establishment block
Brent, Spurlock, Heavrin & Poole, Historic Resource Study, Fort Donelson National Battlefield (Cultural Resource Analysts for NPS, March 2020)

indigenous.html: The park’s 2013 ethnographic overview places the Cumberland valley in a region that archeologists have posited was largely abandoned around 1450–1550; by the 1600s it was a borderland used by at least three tribal nations for hunting and seasonal camps. The Shawnee were among its first occupants, so many that the Cumberland was known as the Rivière des Chaouanons, the Shawnee River; Stewart County was likely a seasonal hunting ground. Around 1714–1715 the Cherokee and Chickasaw drove a large contingent of Shawnee out of the valley. The 1785 Treaty of Hopewell compelled the Cherokee to cede land south of the Cumberland, and in 1805 the Chickasaw reaffirmed a boundary on the ridge between the Cumberland and Tennessee rivers while the Cherokee ceded their lands north of it. By the end of the 1830s the Southeastern nations had been forced to cede their lands east of the Mississippi and remove to Indian Territory, where their governments remain. [1]

sources.title: Lee, Greer & Lee, Fort Donelson National Battlefield: Ethnographic Overview and Assessment, Final Report (Earth Search for NPS, September 2013)

labor_ccc.html: Depression relief programs worked on the park itself. From December 1933 to April 1934, 398 Civil Works Administration laborers, among them African Americans and three women, worked on seven projects in the park, graveling roads, planting and controlling erosion. A crew of four Civilian Conservation Corps enrollees helped historian W. W. Luckett excavate a caved-in magazine at the water batteries; the restored magazine, completed in 1940, is a CCC-built interpretive reconstruction, and the 2020 historic resource study recommends that the park’s National Register listing stop describing it as an original feature. [1]

sources.title: Brent, Spurlock, Heavrin & Poole, Historic Resource Study, Fort Donelson National Battlefield (Cultural Resource Analysts for NPS, March 2020)

slavery.html:
Before the war, the iron furnace companies were Stewart County’s largest slaveholders. The park’s 2020 historic resource study reports that in December 1852 the iron makers on the Cumberland employed 1,395 white workers and 1,910 enslaved laborers, and in 1859 the owners of the Cumberland Iron Works, John and Jane Bell, held 417. Enslaved people made up nearly a quarter of Stewart County’s residents. When rumors of a revolt started at one or more of the furnaces around Christmas 1856 — reports the study calls full of inaccuracies — it was reported that eighty enslaved people were arrested; enslaved furnace workers were beaten to force confessions, and approximately six or seven, possibly more, were killed in Stewart County — though, the study notes, there was no proof of any rebellion. [1]

The fort itself was built by Confederate soldiers and enslaved laborers, who also built more than 400 log huts as the garrison’s winter quarters. [1]

sources.title: Brent, Spurlock, Heavrin & Poole, Historic Resource Study, Fort Donelson National Battlefield (Cultural Resource Analysts for NPS, March 2020)
NPSHistory.com: Fort Donelson NB archive page — overview (from the NPS brochure) and establishment block

women.html:
Enslaved women worked at the iron furnaces, cooking, cleaning, laundering and farming for the works, and the 2020 historic resource study notes that enslaved and free white women also did physically demanding work alongside men at the furnaces; the 417 people held at the Cumberland Iron Works in 1859 included 58 women. After the battle, the brochure notes, women like Mary Ann Bickerdyke nursed sick and wounded soldiers though they were not officially recognized as nurses. [1] [1]

In the contraband camp, women commonly worked as cooks and laundresses, and in March 1864 two women teachers from Wayne County, Indiana, arrived with Ira B. Hutchens to open its school, teaching children and adults to read. [1] [1]

FOFR.summary:
On St. Simons Island, Georgia, at a sharp bend in the Frederica River between salt marsh and live oaks hung with moss, lie the remains of Frederica, the fort and town James Oglethorpe laid out in 1736 to hold Britain’s southern frontier against Spanish Florida. The first settlers — 44 men, mostly skilled workers, and 72 women and children — built palmetto huts and then houses of wood, brick and tabby, a concrete of burnt oyster shell, along a 75-foot-wide Broad Street shaded by orange trees. At its height the town held about 500 people by the 2009 park brochure’s count, more than 800 by the 2016 foundation document’s. [1] [2]

Frederica was born of war. In early 1740 “the aggressive Oglethorpe,” as the 2009 brochure calls him, set out to capture St. Augustine with 900 troops and 1,100 Indian allies, and failed. In July 1742 a Spanish force landed on the island; British troops beat back one column within sight of the town and ambushed another at Bloody Marsh. Casualties were light, but within a week the Spanish withdrew, ending, in the Park Service’s judgment, Spain’s claim to Georgia and the Carolinas. Peace undid the town: the regiment was disbanded in 1749, and a visitor in 1755 found houses without inhabitants and streets overgrown with weeds. [1] [2]

Congress created the national monument on May 26, 1936. Its roughly 282 acres in two units protect a largely intact archeological record — the subject of more than 40 investigations since 1936, with more than 227,000 objects in the park’s collections — and tabby ruins such as the King’s Magazine that now stand in the path of an eroding riverbank. [2]

black.html: Just outside the town wall lies a small cemetery of freed people from the late 1860s and 1870s. One of them is Thomas Abbott, whom Charles Stevens — a coastal shipper who held nineteen people in slavery in 1860 and whose family owned much of the old townsite — had enslaved; another is Celia Abbott. Many freed people, the park notes, still worked for former enslavers after emancipation, often on the same land. Thomas Abbott’s son Robert, born on St. Simons, founded The Chicago Defender, a paper that aided African Americans during the Great Migration and exposed lynching; in 1928 he paid $1,500 for a monument to his ancestors. Ground-penetrating radar in 2017 and 2019 and a 2019 excavation, guided by a church map marking a “Colored burial lot,” confirmed the cemetery’s location. The monument, the 2016 foundation document says, links the park to the island’s African American community and the early struggle against racial prejudice. [6] [2]

sources.title: NPS, Fort Frederica NM: Reconstruction Era History at Fort Frederica (nps.gov, last updated August 1, 2024)
Foundation Document, Fort Frederica NM (NPS, 2016), Other Important Resources and Values: Monuments

climate.html: The river beside which Oglethorpe placed Frederica is now eroding it. The 2016 foundation document warns that shoreline erosion along the Frederica River is an increasing threat, especially to the King’s Magazine, and that a rising water table and more frequent and intense storm surges tied to climate change could disturb buried archeological deposits. Salt marshes on the Georgia coast, it notes, may shrink by 20 to 40 percent this century as sea level rises. The document calls for working with Georgia’s Department of Natural Resources on a Living Shoreline project to stabilize the bank, and one of its interpretive themes concerns conserving and restoring the island ecology that shaped the lives of the people who lived there. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Fort Frederica NM (NPS, 2016), Interpretive Themes; Analysis of FRVs (Archeological Resources, Historic Structures, Frederica River and Salt Marsh); Key Issues: Climate Change

indigenous.html: Before Frederica there was a Guale village on the same ground, allied to Spain through trade and conversion to Catholicism; two Spanish missions stood on the island. The park’s history describes how English traders armed Native slave raiders — the Westo were the largest such group from 1679 into the early 1700s — and how British colonists and their allies attacked the coastal missions to enslave the Guale; in 1683 the village and missions were abandoned, their people following the Spanish south or forcibly removed. Half a century later the Yamacraw, a people of mixed Creek and Yamasee descent, served as treaty negotiators between Oglethorpe and the Creek, allowing Frederica’s peaceful founding in February 1736. Oglethorpe laid out the town lots on a field the Indians had planted in corn, and townspeople traded with Creek and Yuchi people outside the town gate. [3] [1]

sources.title: NPS, Fort Frederica NM: The People Before Frederica (nps.gov, last updated September 12, 2024)
NPSHistory.com: Fort Frederica archive page — 2009 NPS brochure (“Defending Utopia”, “Touring the Park”)

slavery.html: Frederica’s settlers farmed with their own hands, because Georgia banned slavery. The park attributes the ban both to the Trustees’ ideals and to fear: an enslaved person’s quickest way to freedom ran down the Frederica River to Spanish Florida, where accepting Catholicism and fighting for Spain could bring liberty. Colonists petitioned against the ban soon after Frederica’s founding; in 1751 Parliament allowed slavery. By 1775 nearly 18,000 people were enslaved in Georgia; St. Simons came to hold more than 14 plantations. In 1803 John Couper and Thomas Spalding bought 75 Igbo people in Savannah; on the voyage south, the park recounts, they overpowered their captors, took the ship into Dunbar Creek two miles from Frederica, and walked into the water rather than be re-enslaved. Long told as legend — the park notes details vary by source — the event is documented in letters to Pierce Butler, one recording bodies salvaged at ten dollars a head. [1] [5]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Fort Frederica archive page — 2009 NPS brochure (“Defending Utopia”, “The Battle of Bloody Marsh”)
NPS, Fort Frederica NM: Igbo Landing (nps.gov, last updated September 9, 2024)

women.html: Coosaponakeesa, known as Mary Musgrove, was born at Coweta on the Ocmulgee River in 1700, the daughter of British trader Edmund Griffen and of a sister of the Lower Creek leader Brim. When Oglethorpe met the Yamacraw chief Tomochichi in 1733 she interpreted, and the colony paid her one hundred pounds sterling a year. She helped negotiate treaties, recruited warriors against Spain, supplied the struggling colonists with meat and bread, and in 1742 influenced the Creeks to aid the British on St. Simons. She owned three trading posts, and her third husband, Thomas Bosomworth, pressed claims to Sapelo, St. Catherine’s and Ossabaw islands granted to her by the Creeks — making her, in the park’s telling, the largest landowner in colonial Georgia. [4]

FOMC.name: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine
FOMC.summary: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine in Baltimore, Maryland, is the birthplace of the American national anthem. During the Battle of Baltimore on September 13–14, 1814, British naval forces bombarded the star-shaped fort for 25 hours during the War of 1812. The fort's successful defense inspired Francis Scott Key, who watched the bombardment from a truce ship in the harbor, to write the poem "Defence of Fort M'Henry," which was later set to music and became "The Star-Spangled Banner," officially adopted as the national anthem in 1931. Designated as a national park in 1925 and redesignated in 1939, Fort McHenry is the only unit in the National Park System designated both a national monument and a historic shrine.

FORA.summary:
At the wooded north end of Roanoke Island, behind the Outer Banks, English explorers attempted to create England’s first colonial settlement in the New World. In 1585 a military party of 108 colonists built a small earthen fort here and left within a year; in 1587 a second colony of about 110 men, women and children arrived, and when John White returned in 1590 he found only the letters “CRO” carved on a tree and “CROATOAN” carved on a palisade post. Of some 250 colonists who struggled here, 116 men, women and children disappeared. The 355-acre site preserves the reconstructed fort — the only structure whose location is known exactly — and the ground where part, perhaps all, of the settlement stood. [1] [2]

The island holds more than the mystery. The Park Service calls it the site of the first sustained interaction between Native Americans and the English, which produced the first written cultural and ethnographic information of the Algonquian peoples of coastal North Carolina. Created by secretarial order on April 5, 1941, the park had its purpose broadened by Congress in 1990 to include the Native Americans, European Americans and African Americans who lived on the island — among them the 3,500 formerly enslaved people who built the Roanoke Island Freedmen’s Colony during and after the Civil War. [2] [3]

black.html: When Union forces took Roanoke Island in 1862, enslaved people from the island and the surrounding country fled to it — the first group, fifteen or twenty men, women and children, came down the Chowan River. They worked as porters, cooks and laundresses and built forts and docks; men were paid $10 a month and women and children $4. In 1863 Gen. John G. Foster ordered chaplain Horace James to found a colony on the island’s north end, where each family received a one-acre lot. By January 1865 there were at least 591 houses and more than 3,000 residents, with a church, several schools, a steam-powered saw and grist mill, and an appointed council of fifteen. It never became self-sufficient — many of its able-bodied young men enlisted in the Union Army — and James calculated the government owed the freedpeople more than $18,500 in unpaid wages. After the war the island’s prewar residents returned and reclaimed their land, rations were cut, and by February 1867 the colony had virtually dispersed. [3] [2]

sources.title: Treballas & Chapman, Historic Resource Study: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site (NPS, November 1999)
Foundation Document, Fort Raleigh National Historic Site, North Carolina (NPS, July 2017)

climate.html: The island’s history now sits at the water’s edge. The 2017 foundation document reports archeological resources and their context being lost to shoreline erosion, warns that sea level rise may raise the water table and bring saltwater inundation and more severe storms to the earthen fort, and notes that the Waterside Theatre, home of The Lost Colony since 1937, stands directly against an eroding shoreline, where more storm surge, flooding and saltwater intrusion could hasten its decay. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Fort Raleigh National Historic Site, North Carolina (NPS, July 2017)

indigenous.html: The English came ashore among the Carolina Algonquians. In 1584 two of them, Manteo of the Croatoan and Wanchese of the Roanoke, sailed to England with the first expedition, and Thomas Hariot learned some of their language from them. The 1585 colonists, who planted little, came to depend on Indian food, robbed fish traps, and spread measles and smallpox; in 1586, at a parley he had arranged, Ralph Lane’s men opened fire on a prearranged signal and killed and beheaded the Roanoke leader Wingina. In 1587 White’s colonists attacked a village they wrongly believed hostile. Hariot himself rebuked colonists for killing Indians over offenses that might easily have been forgiven. The park’s foundation document concludes that the Carolina Algonquian, a culture nearly 1,000 years old, fell victim to the European race to capitalize on the New World until the culture and its people were extirpated, surviving only in archeological evidence and in the narratives, ethnography and art of the Roanoke voyages. [1] [3] [2]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site archive page — overview (from the 2008 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Treballas & Chapman, Historic Resource Study: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site (NPS, November 1999)
Foundation Document, Fort Raleigh National Historic Site, North Carolina (NPS, July 2017)

labor_ccc.html: The New Deal remade the site before the Park Service owned it. From 1934, relief workers of the Works Progress Administration, under a state commission’s plan with structures designed by Frank Stick, built a juniper-log palisade, blockhouses, a chapel, a museum and other log buildings, several with thatch roofs, as a “highly conjectural” restoration of the 1587 settlement, and in 1937 WPA workers built the Waterside Theatre where Paul Green’s The Lost Colony opened. Visitation rose tenfold, to 30,000 in 1935. But Park Service historian Charles W. Porter found the blockhouse an 18th-century type that would suit the Pennsylvania frontier in 1776 and was absurd as “Fort Raleigh”; the administrative history concludes the log structures were historically inaccurate and had damaged archeologically sensitive ground. [4]

sources.title: Preserving the Mystery: An Administrative History of Fort Raleigh National Historic Site (NPS, 2003), ch. 1 New Deal era

women.html: Raleigh’s second colony was meant to last, and so it carried families: seventeen women and nine children among the 110 colonists, seven of the women probably servants traveling alone. One was Eleanor Dare, John White’s daughter, who on August 18, 1587, gave birth to Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the New World. Nearly three centuries later, women ran the classrooms of the Freedmen’s Colony. Elizabeth James of the American Missionary Association began teaching from a log cabin in October 1863; by fall 1864 the school had seven teachers and still could not keep up with 1,297 children under fourteen and the many adults who wanted to learn to read and write. [3] [2]

sources.title: Treballas & Chapman, Historic Resource Study: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site (NPS, November 1999)

FOSU.summary:
Fort Sumter rises from a human-made island at the mouth of Charleston Harbor: a five-sided, three-tiered masonry fort begun in 1829, after the War of 1812 exposed the weakness of American coastal defenses, and designed for 135 guns and 650 men behind 5-foot walls nearly 55 feet above low water. Enslaved laborers and craftsmen were among those who built it. It was still unfinished when Maj. Robert Anderson moved his garrison there from Fort Moultrie (two companies, 85 men, by the 2013 park brochure’s count) the day after Christmas 1860, six days after South Carolina seceded; the state’s secession declaration objected to a president “whose opinions and purposes are hostile to slavery.” [1] [2]

Confederate batteries opened fire before dawn on April 12, 1861, and after 34 hours Anderson surrendered; no one on either side had been killed. From 1863 Federal guns hurled seven million pounds of metal at the fort over 20 months, and the foundation document calls it the most heavily bombarded location of the entire war, yet its Confederate garrison held until evacuating on February 17, 1865. Across the channel on Sullivan’s Island, the palmetto-log first Fort Moultrie had driven off a British fleet on June 28, 1776; a fort was maintained there until 1947. Congress made Fort Sumter a national monument on April 28, 1948, and redesignated the combined sites a national historical park in 2019. [2] [1] [3]

The park also holds ground where enslaved Africans entered America, and the foundation document says the legacy of their suffering, survival and struggle for freedom continues to define what civil rights and equality mean. [1]

black.html:
When Major Anderson returned to raise the U.S. flag over Fort Sumter on April 14, 1865, three thousand African Americans watched, according to the park’s 2020 administrative history. Among them were the son of Denmark Vesey, executed in 1822 after being accused of trying to lead a slave rebellion in Charleston, and Robert Smalls, with the former Confederate ship he had commandeered and sailed past the fort in 1862, taking his family and other slaves to freedom. [1]

John Tucker, writing in 2002 and quoting historian Thomas J. Pressly, recounts that at the April 1961 centennial in Charleston a Black woman on New Jersey’s centennial commission was denied a room at the headquarters hotel; at the President’s insistence the national assembly moved to the non-segregated naval base, and South Carolina’s commission seceded from the national body and met separately. The fort museum added a section in 1995 on African Americans in the war, highlighting the 54th Massachusetts on nearby Morris Island. [2]

sources.title: Administrative History, Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park, Charleston, SC (NPS, 2020)
Tucker, “Interpreting Slavery and Civil Rights at Fort Sumter National Monument,” The George Wright Forum 19(4), 2002

climate.html: A 2016 Park Service assessment of the park’s 21 structures and 10 roads, parking lots and docks, looking ahead to 2050, found 90 percent of them highly exposed to coastal hazards and sea-level rise. Every asset at Fort Sumter and Liberty Square lies in FEMA’s VE flood zone. Almost two-thirds rated highly vulnerable and only two low; the highly vulnerable assets, Fort Sumter itself among them, carry a replacement value of over $1.1 billion. Three Fort Moultrie assets set on artificial hills received more favorable exposure scores. [1]

indigenous.html: Fort Moultrie holds the grave of Osceola, leader of resistance in the Second Seminole War, who was captured when he went to negotiate under what he believed was a flag of truce and was imprisoned at the fort until his death in January 1838. He was buried without his head. After a man broke into the grave in 1966 meaning to carry the bones to Florida, Park Service historians exhumed it before a crowd of two hundred, found a headless body and the bones of an unidentified infant, displayed the remains for the newspaper and reinterred them in a concrete vault. The park’s 2020 administrative history judges that the publicity surrounding the exhumation suggested a lack of sensitivity to Seminole history. [1]

sources.title: Administrative History, Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park, Charleston, SC (NPS, 2020)

slavery.html:
Charleston was one of North America’s largest slave ports. The park’s Liberty Square visitor center stands on the site of Gadsden’s Wharf, where thousands of enslaved Africans were brought ashore; others landed at quarantine stations on Sullivan’s Island. The 2016 foundation document says roughly 40 percent of all enslaved Africans transported to America disembarked at these sites; the 2020 administrative history reports Charleston historian Nic Butler’s view that the figure is too high for Sullivan’s Island alone, though it may hold for Charleston Harbor as a whole. Arrivals were quarantined in the island’s “pest house,” an average of twelve days, until sold at Charleston’s market. [1] [2]

In 1863 Confederate laborers and slaves inside Fort Sumter worked day and night with cotton bales and sand to buttress the walls facing Federal guns. Fort Moultrie opened its African Passages exhibit on the Middle Passage and slavery in 2009, the year after the Toni Morrison Society placed its first “Bench by the Road” there. [3] [2]

FRRI.name: Freedom Riders National Monument
FRRI.summary: Freedom Riders National Monument in Anniston, Alabama, was designated by President Barack Obama in 2017 to preserve two sites associated with the 1961 Freedom Rides — the former Greyhound Bus Station in Anniston and the site outside the city where a mob firebombed a Greyhound bus carrying Freedom Riders on May 14, 1961. The Freedom Riders were interracial groups of civil rights activists who rode interstate buses into the segregated South to challenge the non-enforcement of Supreme Court rulings that declared segregated public buses unconstitutional. The brutal attacks in Anniston and Birmingham generated national and international outrage and ultimately led the Interstate Commerce Commission to enforce desegregation of interstate travel facilities.

FRST.summary:
Delaware is small, but the Park Service describes it as a state born out of a three-way contest among Sweden, the Netherlands and Great Britain for the Delaware Valley. First State National Historical Park gathers that story in seven places across Delaware’s two northern counties and a corner of Chester County, Pennsylvania: the rocks on the Christina River where Swedish and Finnish settlers landed in 1638; Holy Trinity (Old Swedes) Church, founded by their descendants in 1698; the New Castle Court House and its Green; the Green at Dover; John Dickinson’s plantation; and the 1,359-acre Brandywine Valley tract of farmsteads, wooded hillsides and stream valleys north of Wilmington. Long before any of them, the land was Lenape country. [1] [2]

On December 7, 1787, delegates meeting at the Golden Fleece Tavern on Dover’s Green made Delaware the first state to ratify the Constitution. President Barack Obama proclaimed the First State National Monument on March 25, 2013, and Congress made it a national historical park on December 19, 2014. The park’s own brochure frames its subject as more than 300 years in which people pursued human rights and self-determination on what it calls a fraught and uneven course, marked by questions and contradictions: the plantation of the primary author of the Articles of Confederation had free and enslaved laborers, and the courthouse where Delaware broke with Britain later saw two Quaker abolitionists bankrupted under the Fugitive Slave Act. The Rodneys, like the Ridgelys and the Dickinsons, owned large plantations near Dover; Caesar Rodney was among the leaders of the colony’s independence movement. [1] [2] [3]

black.html:
Delaware’s northern border was the line between slavery and freedom. In December 1845 Samuel D. Burris, a free Black man, guided Samuel and Emeline Hawkins and their six children from Maryland to Quaker John Hunn’s farm; Delaware’s chief justice found no evidence to hold the family, and Thomas Garrett sent them on to Pennsylvania. Convicted in a later case, Burris was sentenced to be sold into slavery for seven years until abolitionists posing as buyers rescued him at auction. In May 1848, in the New Castle Court House, Chief Justice Roger Taney and a jury of Sussex County men described in the study as predominantly pro-slavery found Hunn and Garrett liable under the 1793 Fugitive Slave Act; Taney’s $500 fine per fugitive bankrupted both men. [3] [2]

In the twentieth century, William Poole Bancroft’s Woodlawn Trustees excluded African Americans from their Woodlawn Flats housing in Wilmington, which as late as 1972 allowed only white residents. Only that year, after a decade of Quaker protest and a State Human Relations Commission investigation, did the Trustees agree to accept new applications “without regard to race, color or creed.” [3]

sources.title: Reed & Wallace, A Historic Saga of Settlement and Nation Building: First State National Historical Park — Historic Resource Study (NPS, September 2019)

indigenous.html:
The Lenape knew the Delaware River as the Lenapewihittuck; “Delaware” was an English label — explorers named the bay for Virginia’s governor Lord De La Warr and applied the name to the Lenape themselves. Anthony F. C. Wallace estimated about 8,000 Lenape lived along its drainages around 1600. On the Big Bend of the Brandywine stood Queonemysing, “place where there are long fish,” a summer fishing village. In 1683 Seketarius — a principal Brandywine sachem who, Weslager believed, may have lived there — and other Lenape sachems promised to “give or sell” William Penn the land between the Christina and Upland creeks; in 1701 a Quaker settler was granted the village’s 200 acres on the claim that the people had left — to the surprise, the 2019 study notes, of a band that would have returned the next summer. [3]

Pushed west, the Lenape signed the first treaty the United States made with an Indian nation, at Fort Pitt in 1778. Under two 1829 treaties the federal government removed them to a reservation in Kansas; in 1867 most were moved again to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma), where they live today as the Delaware Tribe of Indians. [3] [2]

sources.title: Reed & Wallace, A Historic Saga of Settlement and Nation Building: First State National Historical Park — Historic Resource Study (NPS, September 2019)

slavery.html: Kent County’s rich soil supported a plantation economy built on enslaved labor, and the John Dickinson Plantation is where the Park Service tells it. The Dickinsons grew wheat and grain there and held a large number of African Americans in bondage. On May 12, 1777, Dickinson signed a deed naming the men, women and children he held — Augustus, Joe, Toby, Mary, Flora, Dinah and many others — and promising them freedom only after another twenty-one years of faithful service. He reconsidered, freeing a few in 1781 and the rest in 1786; by the historic resource study’s count, fifty-nine people in all. Several stayed on as tenant farmers. Slavery remained legal in Delaware throughout the Civil War: nearly 9,000 people, about 15 percent of the state, were enslaved in 1790, and in 1860 there were still more than 1,300 in Sussex County, 303 in Kent and 254 in New Castle. [1] [3]

women.html: In 1920 the Nineteenth Amendment needed one more state, and suffragists hoped it would be the First State. Mabel Lloyd Ridgely, who lived on the Dover Green, had already, with the Colonial Dames, saved the old State House from a demolition the legislature proposed in 1909; she presided over the Delaware Equal Suffrage Association. Seven of the women arrested protesting in front of the White House in 1917 were Delawareans, among them Mabel Vernon and Florence Bayard Hilles. As rival rallies filled the Green, the state Senate ratified on May 5, 1920, but the House tabled the vote after nearly a month of debate — the brochure notes that declining to vote counted as a “no.” Anti-suffragists led by Delawareans Mary Wilson Thompson and Emily Bissell had come to Dover too. Hilles went on to work for passage in Tennessee, which ratified two months later; the amendment became law on August 26. [3] [2]

GATE.summary:
Gateway National Recreation Area wraps around the mouth of New York Harbor, an area known for more than a century as the “Gateway to America.” Its more than 26,000 acres reach from Sandy Hook in New Jersey along the south shore of Staten Island to Jamaica Bay and Breezy Point in New York — about 75 miles of shoreline, 31 of them ocean beach. Assembled from city parks, military posts and undeveloped land, it protects dunes, salt marsh islands and, at Sandy Hook, two globally imperiled kinds of barrier-island forest, maritime red-cedar woodland and maritime holly forest. More than 330 species of birds have been recorded here along the Atlantic Flyway. [1] [2]

The human story is as layered as the shoreline. The Sandy Hook Light, first lit in 1764, is the oldest continuously operating lighthouse in the nation; the Army opened its first weapons proving ground on the Hook in 1874; Fort Wadsworth guarded the Narrows for two centuries; and Floyd Bennett Field opened in 1931 as New York City’s first municipal airport, and during World War II the busiest military airport in the United States. [1] [2]

Congress established Gateway on October 27, 1972, as one of the first urban parks in the National Park System. Its foundation document counts more than 800 historic buildings, structures, landscapes and archeological sites, many already in poor condition when the park inherited them, and names the work ahead plainly: responding to climate change and sea level rise in a park most of whose natural and cultural resources lie beside the ocean and other water bodies. [1] [2]

black.html: Riis Park’s beach was rebuilt by Robert Moses under a 1936 plan, and in 1974 more than three million people visited its mile and a half of sand. When City University sociologists Terry Williams and William Kornblum studied it for the Park Service (the 2000 assessment dates their report to 1975), they found it organized into territories: on summer weekends Bay 5 was the beach of Black and Latin visitors — West Indians, Cubans, Puerto Ricans — with drums, card games and parties into the night; on one July 4th, they numbered perhaps 30,000 across the park. The authors observed pointedly that the crowd hardly matched the middle-class white family the Park Service was comfortable serving, and urged caution before strict enforcement. A 2000 ethnographic assessment for the Park Service found Bays 5 and 6 no longer solely a Black American area but popular with a diverse group of Black Caribbean Americans, Black Americans and Hispanics, a change it tied to twenty-five years of new immigration to Brooklyn and Queens from all over the world. [4] [5]

sources.title: Terry Williams & William Kornblum, Segregation and Use at Riis Park (CUNY Cooperative Park Studies Unit, NPS Research Paper #5, c. 1975), pp. 4–13

climate.html: Most of Gateway’s natural and cultural resources sit beside the ocean and other water bodies, and its 2017 foundation document names responding to climate change and sea level rise as the first of the park’s key issues: the park has been changed by the frequency and intensity of recent storms such as Hurricane Sandy, some sites have already seen more flooding, and the park’s marshes and beaches serve as buffers that protect the neighborhoods behind them. When the document was written the park’s planning was still focused on recovering from Sandy. [2] A park climate poster on Jamaica Bay warns that its salt marsh islands, and the wildlife they shelter, are endangered by sea-level rise and human activity, showing Elders Point in 1951, when its restoration project started in 2006, and as restoration continued in 2010. [7]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Gateway NRA (2017) — Key Issues: Responding to Climate Change and Sea Level Rise
NPS poster, Changes in Sea Level at Jamaica Bay (Gateway NRA, Climate Friendly Parks, undated)

indigenous.html: For thousands of years before the Dutch arrived, the northern shores of Jamaica Bay were home to the Canarsie, and the Rockaway peninsula to the Rechquaakie, “people of the sandy places” — both of the Lenape branch of the Algonquian peoples, according to the Park Service’s 2012 ethnographic overview. They gathered from the bay’s shellfish beds, leaving shoreline middens of oyster shell that the first European writers noticed, and, by early accounts, farmed a great cornfield that stretched for several miles across southeastern Brooklyn. From 1635, when Dutch settlers began building villages on land “purchased” from the Canarsie, warfare, disease and migration steadily weakened the Native communities; the authors date the death of the last known Canarsie person to 1830. Their legacy survives largely in place names: Rockaway, and perhaps Jamaica itself, which the report suggests may come from an old Algonquin word for “place of the beaver.” [3]

sources.title: Kornblum & Van Hooreweghe, The Changing Traditional Uses of Jamaica Bay, New York: Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS Northeast Region Ethnography Program, 2012), ch. 2

labor_ccc.html: The land under Floyd Bennett Field was once Barren Island, for much of the nineteenth century New York City’s offal depot and grease factory. A rendering and fish-oil industry began there in 1845; by 1884 about 500 people worked in its plants, and at its peak in the 1920s and early 1930s the island held close to 1,500 residents — African American, Irish, Italian and Polish families whose children picked over mountains of garbage while their parents worked the try works. The overview dates the eviction of the community to 1936, when Parks Commissioner Robert Moses had it razed for bridge approaches; one former resident, quoted in the overview, remembered only the western half being evicted and about 30 families staying on until 1939. Jane Shaw, for nineteen years the island school’s principal and only teacher, fought for time to let her pupils finish the school year and, in historian Benjamin Miller’s account, succeeded. The 2012 ethnographic overview suggests the eviction stands with the removal of Seneca Village for Central Park, as another example of the powerless being removed to create valuable public places. [3]

sources.title: Kornblum & Van Hooreweghe, The Changing Traditional Uses of Jamaica Bay (NPS, 2012), ch. 2, “The Legacy of Community Solidarity and Defended Neighborhoods”

lgbtq.html: At the eastern end of the beach, Bays 1 and 2 were, in the 1975 study, the home of a large gay community whose use of the beach, Williams and Kornblum reported, already went back more than twenty years; on an average day Bay 1 was about 70 percent gay and Bay 2 about 90 percent. They quoted Arthur Evans, writing in the gay publication The Advocate, on Riis as a haven — one place gay people could be openly themselves. A quarter-century later, the 2000 ethnographic assessment found that Bay 1 had retained its identity as a gay beach. Visitors described it as a space of freedom and liberation, one of the few beaches where they felt safe; some suspected that its neglected bathrooms and missing lifeguard reflected discrimination against them because, as they put it, they were gay and predominantly Black and Latino. In 2025 the Park Service listed Bay 1 as closed to swimming and access because of hazardous erosion. [4] [5] [6]

GLAC.summary:
Glacier National Park protects 1,600 square miles of the northern Rocky Mountains in Montana, where the plains end abruptly against peaks built of sediments laid down 1.5 billion years ago and shoved, about 75 million years ago, over far younger rock along the Lewis Overthrust. From Triple Divide Peak, water runs to the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico and Hudson Bay. Together with Waterton Lakes it is one of the few places in North America where all the native carnivores survive, and George Bird Grinnell named it the Crown of the Continent in 1908. [1] [2]

People have been drawn to this country for 10,000 years, and the park brochure calls it a landscape that has always been sacred to the Blackfeet, Salish and Kootenai peoples. Congress made Glacier the tenth national park on May 11, 1910; in 1932 it and Canada’s Waterton Lakes became the world’s first international peace park, later a biosphere reserve (1976) and World Heritage Site (1995). The park draws more than two million visitors a year; its Going-to-the-Sun Road, which crosses the Continental Divide at Logan Pass, was the first road designated a national historic civil engineering landmark. [2] [1]

The park’s namesakes are leaving. An estimated 150 glaciers existed around 1850; by 2015 only 26 remained large enough to count as active, and the 2016 foundation document describes the last remnants of alpine glaciers as disappearing quickly due to climate change. [4] [2]

climate.html: Glacier’s current ice is geologically young — formed about 7,000 years ago and at its largest around 1850, at the end of the Little Ice Age. Since 1900, the U.S. Geological Survey reports, the park region’s mean annual temperature has risen 1.33 °C, 1.8 times the global mean increase, and rain rather than snow has been the dominant form of the century’s added precipitation. Of the roughly 150 glaciers estimated in 1850, 26 were still active in 2015; Grinnell Glacier lost about 45 percent of its area between 1966 and 2015, and models project that some studied glaciers will disappear between 2030 and 2080. The loss reaches beyond scenery: glaciers act as a bank of water that keeps streams cold and flowing in late summer, and without meltwater, USGS warns, rising stream temperatures could cause local extinctions of sensitive aquatic species and harm the threatened bull trout. [4] [2]

sources.title: USGS, Retreat of Glaciers in Glacier National Park: 1996–2015 (2017), text and Glacier Area Summary table

indigenous.html:
The K’tunaxa (Kootenai) and the Piikáni, one of the three Blackfeet tribes, have ties to this country reaching back well over a thousand years; the mountains are the Piikáni’s most sacred place. On January 23, 1870, in what the 2001 ethnographic overview calls the Massacre on the Marias, Col. E. M. Baker, under orders from General Sheridan, attacked a winter camp of friendly Piikáni and killed 173 or more, mostly women, children and elders. In 1883–1885, as promised rations were delayed or never delivered, 400 to 600 Piikáni died. [3]

In September 1895 three commissioners, George Bird Grinnell among them, met Blackfeet leaders to buy the mountain lands. The Piikáni asked $3 million and received $1.5 million over ten years, plus the right to hunt, fish and cut timber while the land stayed public. The strip became part of Glacier National Park in 1910, and the government came to treat those rights as lost or severely curtailed; many Blackfeet contend they never gave them up. [3]

sources.title: Reeves & Peacock, “Our Mountains Are Our Pillows”: An Ethnographic Overview of Glacier National Park (NPS, 2001), Executive Summary pp. vii–xiii and “The Ceded Strip — 1896,” p. 119

GLCA.name: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
GLCA.summary: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area in southern Utah and northern Arizona encompasses over 1.25 million acres of desert canyon country surrounding Lake Powell, the reservoir created by Glen Canyon Dam on the Colorado River. The dam, completed in 1966, was one of the most controversial reclamation projects in American history — its construction flooded hundreds of miles of canyon and thousands of archaeological sites, galvanizing the modern environmental movement. Author and conservationist Edward Abbey's writings about the area, particularly "Desert Solitaire" (1968), helped bring national attention to the ecological costs of damming western rivers. The recreation area also protects Rainbow Bridge National Monument, one of the world's largest natural bridges, sacred to the Navajo, Paiute, and other Indigenous nations.

GOGA.summary:
Golden Gate National Recreation Area wraps the mouth of San Francisco Bay: more than 80,000 acres across Marin, San Francisco and San Mateo counties, where the San Andreas Fault, the bay at the Golden Gate and the California coastline converge. Its places range from Crissy Field to the former penitentiary on Alcatraz Island, and Muir Woods National Monument, managed as a distinct unit within it, keeps coast redwoods nearly 1,000 years old. The recreation area protects parts of 19 ecosystems and more than 1,250 plant and animal species, and its coastal corridor shelters one of the largest concentrations of rare, threatened and endangered species in the national park system. These lands are the traditional homelands of the Coast Miwok and Ohlone peoples. [1]

The park’s forts and batteries run from Spanish settlement in 1776 to the Cold War Nike missile site in the Marin Headlands; the Presidio was a military post for more than 200 years, under Spain, briefly Mexico, and the United States from 1846. Alcatraz became the nation’s first military prison, then the most notorious maximum-security penitentiary in the United States, then the site of the occupation that helped ignite the movement for American Indian self-determination. In 1972, the year Rep. Phillip Burton warned that unless Congress acted the place where sea, bay and land meet would be doomed, Congress added it and New York’s Gateway National Recreation Area to the park system to bring parks to the people; it was established on October 27, 1972, and now draws more than 17 million visits a year. [2] [1]

black.html: Black soldiers garrisoned the Presidio at the turn of the twentieth century. In 1899 four companies of the 24th Infantry — veterans of Cuba, where they had nursed the sick in the Army hospital and lost many men to disease — arrived in San Francisco, three of them at the Presidio and one on Alcatraz; the 25th Infantry passed through on its way to the Philippines, and the 9th Cavalry was posted at the Presidio in 1900. When President Theodore Roosevelt visited in 1903, two troops of the 9th escorted him, which historian Marvin Fletcher, quoted in Daniels’s 1980 study, called the first instance in the West of Black soldiers holding the position of honor in a public procession. Army-wide, Daniels notes, Black troops in 1908 deserted at a rate under one percent, against nearly five percent among white soldiers. Charles D. Young, a West Point graduate and in 1899 the Army’s only Black commissioned officer apart from chaplains, spoke across the Bay Area. [4] [1]

sources.title: Daniels, Afro-Americans, the San Francisco Bay Area, and the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, 1850–1960 (report for GGNRA, March 13, 1980), pp. 18–21
Foundation Document, Golden Gate NRA (NPS, 2017), p. 4 (Buffalo Soldiers theme)

climate.html: A 2025 coastal hazards assessment for the recreation area, the Presidio and Fort Point looked at 681 buildings and 433 roads, trails, piers and other transportation assets against flooding, shoreline change, sea-level rise and tsunami zones. Most sit high enough to fall outside every hazard zone, but 18 percent are highly or moderately vulnerable, and more than half of those are at Stinson Beach, Crissy Field, lower Fort Baker, Fort Cronkhite, Fort Mason and Point Bonita; the Fort Mason piers and pier sheds and the Alcatraz waterfront are among 18 assets within every hazard zone evaluated. Coastal cliff retreat is a major concern in its own right: it caused the earlier collapse of the Battery Bluff Panama Mounts at Fort Funston and exposes corridors such as Conzelman Road, a main route to Point Bonita and Fort Barry. [5]

sources.title: Peek, Thompson, Tormey & Young, Coastal Hazards & Sea-Level Rise Asset Vulnerability Assessment for Golden Gate NRA, Presidio of San Francisco, and Fort Point NHS: Summary of Results (NPS 641/197620, May 2025), pp. 1–3

indigenous.html:
Before Spain arrived, the San Francisco Peninsula belonged to Ohlone people — called Costanoan, from the Spanish for “coast people,” in Kathryn Lang’s 1979 park study — living in politically autonomous tribelets of roughly 50 to 500 people, averaging about 200; anthropologist Richard Levy put the Ramaytush of San Francisco and San Mateo counties at about 1,400 in 1770. North of the strait, Coast Miwok territory, centered in Marin and Sonoma counties, took in much of today’s park. The Spanish garrison at the Presidio depended on their labor: mission Indians, some lent out and some sent as prisoners for alleged misconduct, built and constantly repaired its crumbling adobe walls and fortifications, with wages paid to the padres rather than the workers. Disease ravaged the missions: Mission Dolores held 1,010 Indians in 1804 and only 241 less than twenty-five years later. [3]

Alcatraz Island, the nation’s first military prison and then a maximum-security penitentiary, later became the site of the occupation that, the park’s foundation document says, helped ignite the movement for American Indian self-determination. [1]

sources.title: Lang, Golden Gate National Recreation Area: The Indian and Hispanic Heritage of a Modern Urban Park (NPS, 1979), pp. 5, 8, 30, 107, 123
Foundation Document, Golden Gate NRA (NPS, 2017), p. 8

latino.html: Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portolá first saw San Francisco Bay in 1769 from Sweeney Ridge, now park land. On June 17, 1776, Lieutenant Moraga led soldiers and settlers out of Monterey for San Francisco, under orders to establish the fort on the site Juan Bautista de Anza had selected: ten leather-jacket soldiers with their families, seven settler families, vaqueros and muleteers. The soldiers were mostly Mexican-born, and Lang’s 1979 study describes most of the colonists as poor families recruited in Sinaloa and Sonora. On September 17, 1776, they formally founded the Presidio of San Francisco with a Mass and the Spanish ceremony of possession. It served Spain, then briefly Mexico, and the United States from 1846, and the park’s foundation document dates its long line of fortifications from that Spanish settlement. [2] [3] [1]

GRCA.summary:
Grand Canyon is a twisting, 277-mile gorge of the Colorado River with thousands of miles of side canyons, carved over six million years. Its walls rise more than a mile above the river and expose one of the most complete geological records on Earth, from flat-lying layers that hold marine fossils down to basement rock as much as 1.84 billion years old. The park’s 1,218,375 acres run from Sonoran Desert at the bottom to conifer forest on the 8,000-foot North Rim, and 94 percent of it is managed as wilderness. [1] [1]

People have lived with the canyon for at least 12,000 years, and eleven federally recognized tribes keep strong historical, cultural and spiritual ties to it; the Navajo, Havasupai and Hualapai reservations share its boundary. President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed 818,560 acres a national monument on January 11, 1908; Congress made it a national park in 1919, and the 1975 Grand Canyon National Park Enlargement Act nearly doubled it, to more than 1.2 million acres. It became a World Heritage Site in 1979, and visitation, averaging about 4.5 million a year, reached 6 million in 2016. [1] [1]

The park’s own brochure points to the pressure on the river: Glen Canyon Dam now releases clearer, colder water in which native fish adapted to warmer, sediment-laden water cannot thrive, and the brochure asks whether one river can meet the Southwest’s growing demand. [1]

climate.html:
Grand Canyon is getting hotter. A 2024 Park Service report finds the park warmed significantly from 1895 to 2020 — 1.89 °F per century on average, and at a rate of 6.31 °F per century since 1970 — while total precipitation did not change significantly. Changes in the region already attributed at least in part to human-caused climate change include drier soils, reduced Colorado River flow and a doubling of the area burned by wildfire across the western United States; drawing on the literature, the report projects more drought, more large fires and worsening threats to archeological sites, cultural landscapes and historic structures. [1]

Mining is the other pressure. In 2012 Interior Secretary Ken Salazar closed federal lands in the Grand Canyon watershed to new mining claims until 2032, partly because, Interior found, impacts to tribal resources likely could not be mitigated. A USGS report published in 2024, co-written by Carletta Tilousi of the Havasupai Tribe, expands the risk framework for uranium mining to include the Havasupai perspective and applies it near Red Butte, a place sacred to the Havasupai, Hopi, Navajo and Zuni. [1]

sources.title: Lawrence et al., Historical and Projected Climate Change for Grand Canyon National Park and Surrounding Areas (NPS NRR 2024/2615), Executive Summary

indigenous.html:
A broken spear point found in Marble Canyon shows a hunter passing through about 11,000 years ago; Puebloan people were farming the rims and river deltas by about 1,500 years ago, and split-twig figurines, masonry rooms and rock art show that the canyon sheltered people for millennia — a span the brochure puts at 600 generations. Eleven tribes — Yavapai-Apache, Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, Kaibab Paiute, Las Vegas Paiute, Moapa Paiute, Navajo, Paiute Indian, San Juan Southern Paiute and Zuni — still use it for trade, gathering and ceremony. [1]

The park itself displaced people. Havasupai families farmed Ha’a Gyoh, below the South Rim, until Park Service policies forced them out in the 1920s; in 2022, at the tribe’s request, the place long called Indian Garden was renamed Havasupai Gardens, and the superintendent called the renaming long overdue. The 1975 enlargement act returned 83,800 acres of park land to the Havasupai Tribe and guaranteed traditional use of another 95,300. [1] [1]

women.html: Four buildings on the edge of the South Rim are the work of Mary Elizabeth Jane Colter, a Pittsburgh-born designer hired by the Fred Harvey Company and the Santa Fe Railway. Her Hopi House (1905) replicated part of the Hopi pueblo at Oraibi; Hermit’s Rest and Lookout Studio (both 1914) took their forms from the landscape, the studio rising out of the rim’s edge — “You can’t imagine what it cost to make it look this old,” she told railroad men who found Hermit’s Rest dingy. For the Desert View Watchtower, completed in 1932, she spent about six months studying ancestral Puebloan tower sites across the Southwest (Anasazi, in the form’s 1986 wording), and its Hopi Room murals are by the Hopi artist Fred Kabotie. A 1986 Park Service nomination argues that her landscape-shaped buildings helped form the architectural aesthetic for development in the national parks. [1]

GRSM.summary:
Great Smoky Mountains National Park spreads across more than 800 square miles of ancient mountains on the North Carolina–Tennessee line, from 850 feet to 6,643 feet at Clingmans Dome. More than 19,000 species have been documented there, and the park brochure counts more tree species than in northern Europe. The Cherokee called these mountains shaconage, “blue, like smoke.” People have lived in and around them for more than 9,000 years. The 2016 foundation document counted about 11 million visitors a year, up from about 9 million for most of the preceding decade. [1] [2]

Amid alarm at commercial logging threats to the forests, Congress authorized the park on May 22, 1926; it was established in 1934, among the first national parks assembled from private lands, bought with money from North Carolina, Tennessee, private citizens and groups, and schools. The cost fell on the people who lived there. Theodore Catton’s 2008 administrative history calls it the largest displacement of resident people in national park history: historian Margaret Brown estimated 5,665 people left some 1,133 farms between the late 1920s and early 1940s, and other estimates run as high as 6,000 to 7,000. A myth born in park circles held that none of the land was condemned; Catton calls it false: both states’ park commissions and the federal government used eminent domain, most often as a threat and sometimes in court. [1] [2] [3]

black.html: The Civilian Conservation Corps in the park was segregated: in March 1935 all 17 CCC companies in the park were white, and Catton writes that it appears no Black company was deployed there. In the fall of 1941, with campground checking stations recording about 200 African American visitors a year, Superintendent J. R. Eakin proposed a separate campground and picnic area for them; Catton reads the aim as keeping the other campgrounds white. The regional director refused, the campgrounds were never segregated, and Catton credits Interior Secretary Harold Ickes, who wanted non-segregation extended to southern parks. In the early 1960s, when nearly every motel and restaurant in Gatlinburg refused Black customers, Superintendent Overly told local owners to open their doors or the government would build a hotel at Sugarlands. The 2016 foundation document still found the park’s interpretation of the African American story inadequate and listed research on that history as a need. [1] [2]

climate.html: The balsam woolly adelgid, an insect from Europe, killed most mature Fraser firs in the park within 45 years, in a park once home to 75 percent of all Fraser firs in the world; the hemlock woolly adelgid has infested and is killing hemlocks throughout the park. A 2010 Park Service briefing reported some of the highest measured air pollution of any national park: 264 unhealthy ozone days since 1997 under the older 85 ppb standard, visible ozone damage on over 30 plant species, worst-day visibility near 15 miles against a natural 77, and twelve Tennessee-side streams listed as impaired for low pH from acid deposition. The 2016 foundation document records a 50-year warming trend, earlier spring warming and later frost, and warns that climate change may shrink the range of some vegetation communities. [1] [2] [3]

indigenous.html: The Cherokee farmed the land, built log homes and used fire to create farmland and improve browse for game; the park brochure says the newcomers took their land, and most members of today’s Eastern Band of Cherokee descend from those not forcibly removed in the 1830s. Catton traces that survival to the Qualla, a band that dissented from the 1835 Treaty of New Echota and resisted removal, and in 1836 entrusted their “white chief,” William Thomas, to win them the right to stay in North Carolina; they received federal recognition as the Eastern Band two years after becoming federal wards in 1868. About 2,200 strong when the park was established in the 1930s, the tribe had about 13,400 enrolled members, on a reservation of some 56,000 acres bordering the park, when Catton wrote in 2008. A park–tribe land exchange first raised in 1931 was concluded only in 1940. [1] [2]

labor_ccc.html: In March 1933 there were 75 men on relief work in the park; within a year and a half there were 4,350, most of them Civilian Conservation Corps enrollees. The park eventually had 22 main CCC camps, more than twice as many as any other unit in the system. Most enrollees were from the South and many from the local area, a substantial number of them mountaineers who lived within the park, and some foremen came from Cades Cove and Smokemont. Crews removed dead chestnut trees, built hundreds of miles of foot and horse trails, campgrounds, a fish hatchery, footbridges and fire lookouts; stone bridges at Sugarlands and the Oconaluftee Ranger Station survive. Some 500 Eastern Band Cherokee sought work in the separate CCC-Indian Division and about 100 found it, mostly on erosion control on Qualla Boundary lands. [1]

sources.title: Catton, A Gift for All Time: Great Smoky Mountains National Park Administrative History (2008)

slavery.html: Abraham Enloe, originally a South Carolinian, acquired land in the Oconaluftee Valley near what historian Robert S. Lambert, writing in 1958, called the Lufty Ranger Station, and most of his nine sons married and settled nearby. In Lambert's account most of the valley's farm labor came from farm families themselves, but “several farmers in the valley were prosperous enough to own a few slaves”: Samuel Sherill and Abraham Enloe each held five enslaved people in 1829. The few people the valley's farmers enslaved, Lambert judged, “seem to have been used for domestic service rather than as field hands.”[1]

GRTE.summary:
With no foothills in the way, the jagged peaks and deep canyons of the Teton Range rise straight out of the valley of Jackson Hole. The rocks at the range’s core, 2.7 billion years old, are among the oldest in North America, yet the mountains are among the youngest in the world: for about 10 million years earthquakes on the Teton fault have lifted the range while the valley floor dropped, until the same rock layers lie nearly 30,000 feet apart. Glaciers up to 3,500 feet thick flowed south from Yellowstone and filled the valley, while alpine glaciers carved the jagged skyline and left moraines that now dam lakes like Jenny Lake. The 310,000-acre park shelters some 1,200 kinds of plants, 300 of birds and more than 60 of mammals. [1]

People have used this valley for roughly 11,000 years, coming seasonally to hunt and gather because the winters were too severe to stay; permanent residents, farmers and ranchers, came only from the mid-1880s. [2] [1] Protecting it took half a century of fighting. Congress created a 96,000-acre park around the peaks and lakes on February 26, 1929. John D. Rockefeller Jr., through the Snake River Land Company, bought more than 35,000 acres of the valley floor, and in 1943 President Franklin Roosevelt proclaimed Jackson Hole National Monument — over strong local opposition, including a heavily armed cattle drive across the monument joined by the actor Wallace Beery. A compromise merged park and monument on September 14, 1950, after Rockefeller gave 32,117 acres to the nation; the HRS calls the result the culmination of 50 years of work, often marred by bitter controversy. [3]

climate.html: Only remnant glaciers remain in the Tetons, and they are shrinking. The park’s 2017 foundation document reports that its glaciers and snowfields are getting smaller each year; records show both advance and retreat, but the overall trend is retreat, and models of Wyoming’s alpine glaciers under projected climate change predict the near-complete disappearance of Teton Glacier within 30 to 75 years. A 1968 USGS map showed 9 named glaciers and about 136 smaller glaciers or perennial snowfields, but the park has never completed a thorough inventory. The same document lists glacier retreat, thinner winter snowpack and lower lake levels among the effects of climate change on the park’s scenery, and notes that landslides and avalanches are exacerbated by increasing climate variability, including more extreme events. [6] The brochure singles out whitebark pine, a keystone food source for grizzly bears and red squirrels, as sensitive to global climate change. [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Grand Teton NP and John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway (2017) — scenic and geologic FRV analyses

indigenous.html:
Jackson Hole’s winters were too severe for year-round living, so for millennia its peoples came in season, following ripening plants and migrating game; the oldest buried cultural deposits in the park date to about 5,850 years ago. The mountain-dwelling people the first trappers met were Eastern Shoshone — the Tukudika, or Sheep-Eaters, who were still without horses when they were placed on the Wind River Reservation around 1868. The Shoshone still keep close ties here: in their belief system high peaks are “Power Mountain,” places to enter the spirit world through visions. [2]

Lt. Gustavus Doane, who led a near-disastrous winter expedition into Jackson Hole in 1876, is part of that history too. [4] In June 2022 Yellowstone’s Mount Doane was renamed First Peoples Mountain; the Yellowstone National Park news release announcing the change states that in 1870 Doane led an attack on a band of Piegan Blackfeet, the Marias Massacre, in which at least 173 people were killed, many of them women, elders and children sick with smallpox, and that he bragged of it for the rest of his life. [5] The Blackfeet are among the tribes Grand Teton lists as traditionally associated with the park. [6]

labor_ccc.html: When the Bureau of Reclamation dammed Jackson Lake, the shoreline trees were flooded and killed, and dead and downed trees ringed the lake. Clearing them was one of the Civilian Conservation Corps’ biggest undertakings in the valley. Young men aged 17 to 25 were stationed in camps at Leigh Lake, Lizard Point and near Colter Bay, and from 1934 at Camp NP-4 at the south end of Jenny Lake, manned through 1942. Between 1933 and 1937 they cleared the bulk of 7,000 acres of shoreline; by September 1936 crews were finishing the last 85 acres. They also built the Jenny Lake campground, trails to Phelps Lake and Garnet Canyon, telephone lines and staff housing, and several buildings from the Jenny Lake camp, meant to be temporary, were moved elsewhere and, the HRS reports, remain in use. [3]

GWMP.summary:
George Washington Memorial Parkway runs along the Potomac River through Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia, protecting the river’s landscape and natural shoreline while offering scenic vistas of Washington, D.C., and the Great Falls of the Potomac. Congress established it on May 29, 1930, through the Capper-Cramton Act. Its first leg, the Mount Vernon Memorial Highway, opened in 1932, the bicentennial of Washington’s birth; the 2014 foundation document calls it the first comprehensively designed modern motorway built by the federal government, a pioneer of limited access, grade-separated intersections and cloverleaf interchanges. The northern section was completed in 1962, and the Maryland side was renamed Clara Barton Parkway in 1989. [1] [1]

The park covers 7,600 acres by the park brochure’s count (7,374 in the foundation document) and more than 25 sites. [1] At Great Falls, the largest waterfall on the Potomac, the river rushes over jagged rocks into Mather Gorge beside the remnants of the Patowmack Canal, whose construction Washington presided over; the 15-mile Potomac Gorge is, in the foundation document’s words, one of the most biologically diverse natural areas in the national park system. Fort Hunt Park, once part of the Mount Vernon estate, had batteries that defended the river during the Spanish-American War; in World War II, as the site of P.O. Box 1142, it served as a prisoner-of-war camp and the interrogation center for many high-profile German prisoners. [1]

The parkway’s lands hold prehistoric American Indian sites, and it also manages Theodore Roosevelt Island, a Civil War training area for the Union Army that included the first United States Colored Troops, and Clara Barton National Historic Site at Glen Echo. [1]

black.html: In 1863 the island, then called Analostan or Mason’s Island, became Camp Greene, where the 1st Regiment of United States Colored Troops was mustered. The Emancipation Proclamation had opened Union enlistment to African Americans that January, but Black soldiers could not rise to officer rank and were paid seven dollars a month against thirteen for white soldiers of equal rank. The District of Columbia mustered the regiment in May 1863, and some 3,500 Black men from the District enlisted by the war’s end. Walt Whitman visited and called it the pleasantest camp he had yet seen. On July 30, 1863, the regiment left the island for the siege of Richmond and Petersburg, later fought at Wilmington, and lost 185 enlisted men before it was decommissioned in 1865. [1]

sources.title: NPS, Camp Greene (nps.gov/this, last updated May 23, 2024)

indigenous.html: Theodore Roosevelt Island lies in a stretch of the Potomac valley that people have used for over 15,000 years, a Park Service history of the island explains. Projectile points about 9,000 years old are its earliest archeological record; people came to fish, hunt, gather shellfish and nuts, and, archeologists suspect, revisited such camps over generations. Around 4,000 years ago people of the Savannah River Culture brought soapstone bowls, and settlement on the island peaked in the Middle Woodland period (700 B.C.E.–1000 C.E.). By the Late Woodland the region’s tribes included the Powhatan coalition in Virginia and the Piscataway and Nanticoke in Maryland, and John Smith’s map of 1607–08 records the nearby settlements of Namoraughquend and Nacotchtanck. English encroachment disrupted the economies and social structures of Virginia tribes, the history notes, yet many Native people still live in the Potomac valley. [1] The foundation document records American Indian archeological sites along the parkway, including on the bluff at Clara Barton’s house. [1]

sources.title: NPS, A History of Native American Life on Theodore Roosevelt Island (nps.gov/this, last updated May 23, 2024)

labor_ccc.html: In May 1933 about 3,000 delegates to a second Bonus March of World War I veterans were bused to Fort Hunt, where Eleanor Roosevelt visited them; when Franklin Roosevelt offered places in the new Civilian Conservation Corps, 2,657 enrolled. CCC Camp NP-6 opened there on October 17, 1933, with 200 enrollees of Company 1241 from New York and Virginia, who cleared dead timber, built bridle paths and landscaped the capital’s parks. A third march camped at Fort Hunt in May 1934, including 270 African American delegates, and 565 more veterans joined the Corps. Company 2387, which replaced it in 1937, planted trees and shrubs along the parkway, and between 1933 and 1938 some 20 enrollees built relief maps and models of parks in Fort Hunt’s “Model Laboratory.” [1] On Theodore Roosevelt Island, CCC crews from 1935 graded paths and, with the Historic American Buildings Survey, excavated the Mason House foundation in 1936. [1]

sources.title: Matthew R. Laird, “By the River Potomac”: An Historic Resource Study of Fort Hunt Park (NPS, August 2000), ch. 5

women.html: Clara Barton’s house at Glen Echo, Maryland, went up in 1891 on land given by developers Edward and Edwin Baltzley, who also supplied the labor and some of the materials, hoping her fame would sell lots around their Chautauqua. Barton — Civil War nurse, women’s rights suffragist, and founder and first president of the American Red Cross — lived there briefly in 1891 and again from 1897 until her death in 1912, kept a small farm of cows, horses, chickens and goats, and presided over the Chautauqua’s Women’s Executive Committee. [1] The house was the Red Cross’s first permanent headquarters from 1897 to 1904. The foundation document notes that Barton won international recognition at a time when women were not given the same opportunities as men, and that the site, established in 1974, was one of the first national historic sites dedicated to the accomplishments of an American woman. [1]

HAFE.summary:
At Harpers Ferry the Potomac River cuts through the Blue Ridge and takes in the Shenandoah, leaving a V-shaped water gap that Thomas Jefferson called perhaps one of the most stupendous scenes in nature, worth a voyage across the Atlantic. That gap made the place a crossroads from the earliest human habitation onward: American Indians first, then European settlers, and in 1747 Robert Harper’s ferry across the Potomac. Congress authorized a federal armory here on June 15, 1796; when production began in 1801 it was the nation’s second, and in its workshops new ideas about interchangeable parts were tried and tested while large-scale manufacturing turned a quiet rural village into one of the leading industrial centers of its day. [1] [2]

In October 1859 John Brown and his followers seized the armory, determined to arm enslaved people and spark a rebellion; the raid failed, but his trial and execution, in the park brochure’s words, propelled the nation toward civil war. Harpers Ferry then changed hands eight times, and in September 1862 Stonewall Jackson captured nearly 12,700 Union soldiers here — the largest surrender of U.S. troops in the war. After it, Storer College opened on Camp Hill in 1867 as a school primarily for formerly enslaved people, and in 1906 hosted the second conference of the Niagara Movement, where W. E. B. Du Bois demanded equality and civil rights. Congress authorized Harpers Ferry National Monument in 1944; it became a national historical park in 1963 and now covers 3,745 acres in West Virginia, Maryland and Virginia. [1] [2]

black.html:
During and after the war, people escaping slavery, called “contrabands,” poured into Harpers Ferry; by the mid-to-late 1860s about 700 African Americans lived in town, double the prewar number. Freewill Baptists opened a school for refugees in the armory paymaster’s Lockwood House in 1864, and on October 2, 1867, Storer College began classes there with nineteen students. Students were bullied by local residents and at times had to be escorted into town by hired militiamen. For 25 years Storer was the only institution in West Virginia offering African Americans secondary and post-secondary education; Frederick Douglass was among its first trustees. [3] [2]

In August 1906 the Niagara Movement held its second conference at Storer, and participants walked from the college to John Brown’s Fort, then standing on the Murphy Farm, going barefoot as they approached it to commemorate Brown; the conventions led to the founding of the NAACP in 1909. Storer closed in 1955, after the State of West Virginia withdrew its support. [3] [2]

sources.title: Bailey, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment Study of Harpers Ferry NHP (NPS, 2017), pp. 27, 47–49, 107, 140
Foundation Document, Harpers Ferry National Historical Park (NPS, 2016), pp. 4, 6

indigenous.html: People first lived in the Shenandoah Valley in the Paleoindian period, roughly 11,000 to 9,600 B.C. A 1989–1990 excavation in Lower Town recovered 1,585 artifacts — ceramics, stone tools, postholes and hearths — from Late Archaic and Early Woodland occupations around 1200 to 500 B.C. By the time Europeans arrived about 1600, the valley had held no permanent villages for nearly a century; Tuscarora and Shawnee people lived there in temporary settlements, and Iroquois raiding parties used it as a route to attack southern nations such as the Catawba and Cherokee. A series of treaties pushed Native nations west; in the 1744 Treaty of Lancaster the Iroquois sold their land claims to the Virginia Colony and moved west of the Allegheny Mountains. The 2017 ethnographic overview could identify no Native American groups with ties to the park’s resources, quotes an earlier park study that there are no federally recognized tribes in the vicinity, and acknowledges that the park has generally devoted more of its resources to the town’s historic remains than to its pre-contact past. [3]

sources.title: Bailey, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment Study of Harpers Ferry NHP (NPS, 2017), ch. 2, Native American Presence, pp. 15–18

labor_ccc.html: The armory began in 1801 with 28 armorers who turned out 293 flintlock muskets that year; by 1810 it employed almost 200 workers in 28 buildings. Its earliest workforce was mostly highly skilled gunsmiths using hand tools, each able to make an entire gunstock or forge and assemble a whole musket lock, and the Ordnance Department’s drive to impose factory discipline met resistance. When Superintendent Thomas Dunn posted strict rules and inspections that cut piece-work wages, a disgruntled former worker Dunn had refused to rehire, Ebenezer Cox, murdered him in his office in early 1830; Cox’s execution, the park’s 2006 study says, made him a folk hero to the armorers. In 1842, after Major Henry Craig imposed a fixed workday enforced by a clock, the entire workforce struck for a week and sent a delegation to President John Tyler protesting that they were being made into “mere machines of labor.” The protest failed: Congress passed, and Tyler signed, a law placing military superintendents over all U.S. armories and arsenals. [4]

sources.title: Lee, The U.S. Armory at Harpers Ferry: Historic Resource Study (NPS, 2006), pp. 12, 23, 30, 42–43

slavery.html:
Harpers Ferry sat in Jefferson County, Virginia, which in the first half of the nineteenth century held twice as many enslaved people as any other county in present-day West Virginia: 4,157 in 1840, 4,341 in 1850, and 27 percent of the population by 1860. In Harpers Ferry and Bolivar most owners held one or two people. Newspaper accounts cited in the 2017 ethnographic overview show people bought and sold frequently; an 1857 notice reported free Black people sold by court order in front of the Charles Town courthouse for remaining in the state contrary to law; and escapes toward Pennsylvania were frequent enough that the Virginia Slave Insurance Company was formed in Charles Town to insure against them. [3]

On October 16, 1859, Brown led 21 men against an arsenal holding 100,000 arms. The first man killed was Heyward Shepherd, an African American baggage handler for the B&O Railroad. By noon on October 17, the park’s own 2006 armory study records, drunken vigilantes encircled the armory and several captured raiders were brutally executed; U.S. Marines took Brown at daybreak on October 18. [3] [4]

HOBE.name: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park
HOBE.summary: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park in east-central Alabama preserves the site of the decisive battle of the Creek War. On March 27, 1814, forces led by General Andrew Jackson, including U.S. Army regulars, Tennessee militia, Cherokee allies, and Lower Creek warriors, attacked the fortified camp of the Red Stick Creek faction at a horseshoe-shaped bend on the Tallapoosa River. Approximately 800 of the 1,000 Red Stick warriors were killed in the battle — one of the deadliest defeats suffered by Native Americans in U.S. history. The resulting Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Creek Nation to cede roughly 23 million acres — half of present-day Alabama and part of southern Georgia — to the United States. The park was established in 1956.
