HOFU.summary:
In 1771, as relations between England and its American colonies came apart, Mark Bird, already an important figure in the colonial iron industry, built Hopewell Furnace in eastern Pennsylvania. It took an acre of woodland to make enough charcoal to run an iron furnace for a single day. When the Revolution came, Bird turned from casting stove plates to supplying cannon and shot to the Continental Army and Navy; afterward trouble collecting debts from the new nation, a postwar depression and a 1786 flood added to his financial woes, and Hopewell was sold at a sheriff’s sale in 1788. [1]

The furnace’s best years came under resident manager Clement Brooke, from 1816 to 1831, when its iron went up and down the East Coast. The Panic of 1837, the Bessemer steel process and the rise of urban steel mills ended that, and Hopewell went out of blast for the last time on June 15, 1883. Around it had lived what historians call an “iron plantation”: miners, woodcutters, colliers, teamsters, moulders and farmers whose lives the furnace governed, African Americans among them, enslaved at first and later free. [1]

The federal government bought the property in 1935, and on August 3, 1938, 214 acres of furnace lands were set aside as a national historic site — according to the park’s 2004 historic resource study, the first industrial complex the Park Service established as a historic site. The 2017 foundation document describes an iron-making village that operated from 1771 to 1883, whose buildings, landscape and people illustrate the American industrial past, and whose surviving company records reveal the daily business and the activities of the people who lived and worked there. [1] [1] [1]

black.html:
An African American community grew up along Six Penny Creek, in what is now French Creek State Park; an 1860 map shows about a dozen families there. Peter Jones and Joseph Tolbert, of two of those families, probably worked at Hopewell — Jones as early as 1818 — and the 2004 historic resource study judges the community likely to have been formed by people who escaped slavery. By 1856 it had its own church, Mount Frisby African Methodist Episcopal, on land owned by Isaac Cole; it served as a stop on the Underground Railroad. Cole and James Jackson, both Union Army veterans, are buried in its cemetery, which the study calls the oldest African American cemetery in Berks County. Furnace records name many other African Americans, among them Bill Jacobs, who spent nearly 100 years at Hopewell as teamster, coachman and gardener. [1]

In 1988 superintendent Derrick Cook began an annual Black History Month program at the site. [1]

labor_ccc.html:
Before the government had finished buying the land for the French Creek Recreational Demonstration Area, a Depression program to give poor city dwellers outdoor recreation, Civilian Conservation Corps Company 2213, 200 unemployed young men, arrived at Camp SP-7 on December 10, 1934. In little more than six months they replaced roofs and stabilized five structures of the old iron plantation for their own use. In April 1935 CCC architect Gustavus Mang reported on the site’s history and recommended preserving the furnace buildings. [1] [1]

The 2004 historic resource study is frank about the cost: enrollees used slag piles and stones from the East Head Race walls to build roads, regraded ground near the Ironmaster’s House, reportedly removed artifacts and disposed of some furnace records — perhaps, it says, the most damaging act. The Park Service adds that CCC workers stabilized the furnace stack, built Route 345 and served as some of the site’s first tour guides. [1] [1]

slavery.html:
When Pennsylvania passed its emancipation act in 1780, Mark Bird held 18 enslaved workers, which the park’s 2004 historic resource study says made him the largest slaveholder in Berks County. Some of them worked at his Birdsboro forges, and tradition holds that enslaved laborers dug the furnace’s East Head Race. The study notes this was not unusual: travelers reported that enslaved African Americans did much of the work at Maryland’s ironworks, and enslaved workers were known at furnace jobs in southeastern Pennsylvania in the 1750s. [1]

The park brochure traces the change over time: African Americans worked the furnaces enslaved at first, later as temporarily employed runaway slaves and as free Black workers. The 2017 foundation document lists enslaved people, the Underground Railroad, abolition and emancipation among the stories of the park’s interpretive themes. [1] [1]

women.html:
The furnace’s workforce was not only men. The park brochure says the cleaners who finished cast products were often women and children, that women added to family incomes by sewing, lodging and boarding single workers and laundering, and that some earned extra income as woodcutters and miners. The 2017 foundation document calls for showing women at Hopewell in roles ranging from traditional nineteenth-century ones to work directly involved in iron making. [1] [1]

Elizabeth Disrude, superintendent from October 1975 to February 1988, was the Mid-Atlantic Region’s first female superintendent. Glaser’s 2005 administrative history reads her appointment as part of the Park Service’s response to the women’s rights movement, and notes that the 1970s living-history program brought in women’s roles, though usually closer to the period celebrated by the Bicentennial than to the site’s own period of interpretation. [1]

HUTR.summary:
Hubbell Trading Post sits at 6,325 feet beside the Pueblo Colorado Wash on the edge of Ganado, Arizona, in a valley the Navajo call Lók’aah niteel, Wide Reeds, and in the middle of the Navajo Nation. People lived along this wash long before any trader: Wide Reed Ruin, a pueblo with kivas and plazas inside the site, was built in A.D. 1276–77 by tree-ring dating, and, by the administrative history’s account, the general area was largely abandoned about 1300 because of a drought that had begun in the 1270s. [1] [1] [1]

John Lorenzo Hubbell, born in Pajarito, New Mexico Territory, in 1853, began trading in the Ganado valley in 1876 and, by the park’s administrative history and foundation document, bought a trading post on this spot — William Leonard’s, the administrative history says — in 1878 (the 2010 park brochure dates the purchase to 1876). He came as the Navajo struggled to adjust to reservation life after the Long Walk. In 1883 he built a new post of uncoursed sandstone, today divided into a bullpen store, jewelry room and rug room beside a wareroom, and a U.S. post office opened there in the 1880s. At various times Hubbell and his sons owned more than 30 trading posts. He died in 1930 and lies in an unmarked grave on Hubbell Hill, following Navajo custom. [1] [1] [1]

Congress authorized the historic site on August 28, 1965, on the understanding that it would stay a working business, and Dorothy Hubbell sold it to the Park Service in 1967. It is the oldest continuously operating trading post in the Southwest: artisans still bring in rugs, jewelry, pottery and baskets, neighbors still buy groceries, and the museum collection holds more than 450,000 items. [1] [1]

indigenous.html:
In 1864 the U.S. Army forced more than 8,500 Diné (Navajo) on the Long Walk to Hwééldi — Bosque Redondo, at Fort Sumner, New Mexico Territory — for four years of imprisonment. When they came home in 1868 their hogans, herds and crops were gone, and many came to depend on traders for food. The Navajo leader Totsonii Hastiin, Ganado Mucho, invited Hubbell to the valley; when smallpox swept the reservation in 1886 Hubbell turned his home into a hospital. Traders wrote letters and served as pawnbroker and banker; the Manchesters’ 1993 administrative history counts them among the most important acculturating forces in Navajo history. [1] [1] [1] [1] [1]

The park brochure says Navajo learned weaving from Spanish, Mexican and Pueblo weavers and surpassed them, and dates blankets of Spanish Churro-sheep wool to the 1650s; Navajo-Churro ewes still lamb at the post each spring. Hubbell urged weavers toward older patterns in gray, black, white and red, the style now called Ganado Red. Daghaa Neezi, Friday Kinlicheenie, came to work at the post around 1915, kept its garden for some 70 years and, as a medicine man, performed a Blessing Way there. [1] [1] [1]

latino.html: Hubbell came from a Hispanic New Mexican family on his mother’s side. His father, James Lawrence Hubbell, came from Connecticut; his mother, Julianita Gutierrez (so spelled in the administrative history; the park brochure has “Gutierriez”), was of Spanish descent. He worked as a clerk and Spanish interpreter at forts and trading posts before he traded, married Lina Rubi of Cebolleta, New Mexico Territory, in 1879, and was known to local Hispanics as Don Lorenzo — “Don,” the administrative history notes, being a Spanish term of respect — and to the Navajo as Naakaii Sani, Old Mexican. [1] [1]

women.html: Born Dorothy Elizabeth Smith in Indiana, Dorothy Hubbell came west in 1920 to teach the Hubbell children and soon married their widowed father, Roman. By 1957, with Roman gradually paralyzed by strokes and the family company in bankruptcy, she was running the post while caring for him. That July she asked the Museum of Northern Arizona whether it could acquire and preserve the place; it could not, but the administrative history dates the movement for a national historic site to that year. She was appalled when one prospective buyer said he would sell off the contents and put in a liquor store, and the Manchesters credit her “vision, determination, and patience” for bringing the collection to the American people intact. [1] [1] [1]

INDE.summary:
Independence National Historical Park covers more than 51 acres of downtown Philadelphia, and at its center stands the old Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall. In its Assembly Room the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776; four days later the Declaration was read aloud to the public for the first time in the square outside. In 1787 fifty-five delegates were sent to Philadelphia, and in the same Assembly Room they created the Constitution — a document, the park’s own brochure says, that failed to adequately address slavery. Congress sat in nearby Congress Hall from 1790 to 1800, while Philadelphia was the nation’s capital, and the First Continental Congress had gathered at nearby Carpenters’ Hall in 1774. [1] [1]

The bell that hung in the State House steeple was first heard in 1753; its inscription reads “Proclaim Liberty throughout All the land unto All the Inhabitants Thereof.” In the 1830s anti-slavery groups named it the Liberty Bell; it cracked around 1846. The park’s brochure calls the crack a reminder that liberty is imperfect, hopefully evolving to include those denied full participation. [1] [1]

Congress created the park on June 28, 1948. The park was made by creating public parks and open green space around the founding-era landmarks, clearing later commercial buildings, drawing on the City Beautiful movement and the colonial revival of Williamsburg, and in the 1950s and 1960s park architects, archeologists and historians working on Independence Hall developed restoration methods the Park Service still treats as a model. Independence Hall was named a World Heritage Site in 1979. [1] [1] [1]

black.html: Ona Judge hid among the free Black Philadelphians she had befriended — part of a city the brochure describes as home to people fleeing slavery and free people of African descent. The house itself was torn down in 1832, and for some fifty years after Independence Mall was built the site lay under a lawn and a women’s restroom, marked only by a small brass plaque. In 2002 independent scholar Edward Lawler Jr. showed that Washington had ordered a smokehouse on the lot altered as housing for his “stablepeople.” Lawler judged it most likely that the order was carried out and the building housed enslaved stable workers, and he pointed out that visitors would pass over that site on entering the new Liberty Bell Center; in the controversy that followed, attorney Michael Coard founded the Avenging the Ancestors Coalition, and on July 3, 2002, some five hundred mostly African American protesters demanded a memorial. The 2007 excavation uncovered the kitchen where Hercules cooked and drew more than 300,000 visitors in four months; the park then built its first community-based exhibit there, interpreting race and slavery. [1] [1] [1]

slavery.html: Partly beneath today’s Liberty Bell Center stood the President’s House, the executive mansion of George Washington (1790–1797) and John Adams (1797–1800). The Washingtons brought nine enslaved Africans from Mount Vernon to work there at various times: Austin, Christopher Sheels, Giles, Hercules, Joe Richardson, Moll, Ona (Oney) Judge, Paris and Richmond. Under Pennsylvania’s Gradual Abolition Law of 1780, the park’s 2009 excavation report (revised 2023) explains, enslaved people became free after a six-month stay in the state, so Washington rotated them back to Virginia — a practice the report says itself violated Pennsylvania law, which was not enforced. In the spring of 1796 Ona Judge walked out while the family sat down to dinner and escaped to New Hampshire; she died free in 1848. Hercules, the chef, escaped from Mount Vernon on February 22, 1797. Adams, the brochure notes, never owned slaves. [1] [1]

women.html: Lucretia Mott and other activists of the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society wrote for The Liberty Bell, the Boston abolitionist annual that in 1839 first gave the bell its name in print and for twenty years used it as an anti-slavery symbol, John Paige’s special history study for the park records. On July 4, 1876, Susan B. Anthony gave the first public reading of a women’s declaration of rights here, urging suffrage. And on August 2, 1954, the General Federation of Women’s Clubs gave the Park Service $209,541.82 raised nationwide to restore and refurnish the first floor of Independence Hall — by the park’s account the largest single sum ever applied to the building to that time. [1] [1] [1]

INDU.name: Indiana Dunes National Park (National Lakeshore)
INDU.summary: Indiana Dunes National Park on the southern shore of Lake Michigan in northwestern Indiana protects 15,349 acres of dunes, wetlands, prairies, rivers, and forests. The park's origins trace to the early 20th-century conservation campaign led by botanist Henry Cowles, whose groundbreaking studies of plant succession on the Indiana dunes helped establish the modern science of ecology. Despite being surrounded by one of the most heavily industrialized regions in North America, the park supports remarkable biodiversity — over 1,100 native plant species, the fourth-highest count of any national park unit. Originally designated as Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore in 1966, it was redesignated as a national park in 2019.

JELA.summary:
This land is the creation of the Mississippi River. At the end of its journey it drops sediment scoured from 40 percent of the continental United States, and the ground beneath the New Orleans region is less than 4,000 years old — marsh, slow bayous, cypress swamp and forested natural levees in a restless interplay of land and water. American Indians settled the delta as it formed, some 2,500 years ago; from the 1720s European settlers and enslaved Africans took their place among them, and the park’s brochure traces how French colonists, the Chitimacha, Houma and other tribes, enslaved West Africans, Spanish-speaking Isleños, free people of color from the Caribbean and Acadians each shaped the delta’s culture. [1]

On January 8, 1815, on the Chalmet plantation below New Orleans, Andrew Jackson’s mixed force of regulars, militia, volunteers and Jean Lafitte’s Baratarian privateers stopped a British assault in less than two hours; more than 2,000 British soldiers were killed, wounded or captured and American casualties numbered fewer than 20. Chalmette National Historical Park, created in 1939 to preserve part of that field, was the first national park unit in Louisiana. Congress expanded it into Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve on November 10, 1978, and in 1988 added three Acadian cultural centers, for six sites in all. The land itself is now going: human engineering has blocked sedimentation and increased coastal erosion, and rising seas due to climate change are accelerating the loss, by the brochure’s count a football field’s worth of land every 45 minutes. [1] [2]

black.html: Around 1867, Jean Pierre Fazende, a free man of color before emancipation, began selling lots on part of the old Chalmet plantation to freedmen. Fazendeville grew into a close-knit Black working-class village of about 40 houses, a church, stores, a school and benevolent societies, sitting between the battlefield monument and the national cemetery, which for generations drew its laborers from the village. Blythe’s 2012 administrative history records that NPS managers believed from the start that the community would have to be obliterated to provide a meaningful visitor experience of the historic scene. A 1962 law authorized the federal government to acquire every property in the village, and by 1964 the community was lost. The taking came, Blythe notes, while Black residents of St. Bernard Parish were struggling to register to vote, and some of those displaced saw the two as connected. The same history notes that throughout the Jim Crow era park managers and the major New Orleans media often overlooked the free men of color who helped win Jackson’s victory. The NPS placed a wayside about Fazendeville on the battlefield in 2008. [3] [2]

climate.html: The delta was always in motion: over 3,500 years the Mississippi built five major deltas, the newest only 500 years old, while subsidence and erosion balanced the new land it laid down. Human engineering, from artificial levees to jetties, has upset that balance. The park’s 2015 foundation document says parts of this landscape have the highest rate of relative sea-level rise and land loss in North America — a historical average of 0.36 inches a year at Grand Isle from 1947 to 2012, with NOAA-based projections for 2100 of 3.30 to 7.62 feet. In Barataria Preserve, scientists have already documented species lost from the natural levee ridges, more flooding and land loss, and the document names the climate-driven rise of ocean influence over the delta and its people the park’s major cross-cutting concern. [1] [2]

indigenous.html: People lived in the Barataria basin as soon as the river formed it, and by the Marksville period (about 100 B.C. to A.D. 300) were building large villages, growing corn and probably beans and squash to a moderate extent while hunting and gathering remained their most important source of food. Prehistoric shell middens from that long occupation remain part of the preserve’s landscape. At French contact their descendants were the Washa, Chawasha and Chitimacha (“Sitimachas” on an early French map after Guillaume Delisle). France’s Indian allies waged a twelve-year war on the Chitimacha, and, Holmes writes, Chitimacha bands contributed many Indian slaves to the French colony; the 1718 peace forced the Chitimacha to abandon Bayou Lafourche and settle near New Orleans. By 1739 the Washa and Chawasha together numbered only thirty warriors, which, Holmes writes, probably reflects significant population loss from disease. [4] [2]

latino.html: Spain took over Louisiana in 1763, and its colonial government built the public road it named El Camino Real de Barataria, the royal road, a remnant of which survives in the preserve. In 1778 the first settlers from the Canary Islands — the Isleños — arrived, brought by the Spanish governor to strengthen Spain’s presence and provide a barrier against British and American aggression. In 1779 the Spanish government settled a group of about 150 on a grant that took in the meeting of Bayou des Familles and Bayou Barataria; John McDonogh, who later bought the abandoned grant, said the bayou was called “des Familles” after the Canarian families placed there. Repeated floods from hurricanes and river crevasses, and a gradual drift of settlers to other Canarian settlements, wore the settlement down over some sixteen years, until a crevasse that opened in or before 1796 ruined the last five families’ crops and livestock and the government moved them to Terre aux Boeufs, in today’s St. Bernard Parish. [1] [2] [4]

slavery.html: Before the Civil War the Barataria region near New Orleans was worked as sugar plantations. In 1850, Holmes’s 1986 historic resource study counts 1,176 people living there: 504 enslaved, 15 free people of color and 657 white, with 79 percent of the enslaved owned by planters and living on the plantations. In 1856 the Mavis Grove plantation inventoried houses for 156 enslaved people alongside a steam-powered sawmill and seventy mules; the Andrew Hodge estate, almost entirely Mavis Grove, was valued at $226,914.61. Enslaved workers usually labored six days a week for their owners, and every day during the October-to-December harvest and sugar making. Earlier, from 1805 to 1813, Jean Lafitte, who the park’s foundation document says navigated these swamps smuggling contraband and enslaved people, built a commercial empire in the basin and, Holmes writes, dared to openly advertise an auction of contraband slaves there. [4] [2]

LOWE.summary:
The Merrimack River drops ninety feet over its last forty-eight miles, and more than a third of that fall comes in one mile near its junction with the Concord: Pawtucket Falls. In November 1821 Nathan Appleton, Patrick Tracy Jackson, Kirk Boott, Paul Moody and Warren Dutton walked the grounds at East Chelmsford. Within a year their “Boston Associates” controlled the 400 acres between the Pawtucket Canal and the two rivers; in 1822 the Merrimack Manufacturing Company was chartered, and by 1836 Lowell was the third incorporated city in Massachusetts, with 17,000 people and eight major textile mills employing 7,500 workers. [1]

The park’s 2017 foundation document says Lowell was not, as is sometimes claimed, the birthplace of America’s Industrial Revolution, but the place where its developments converged on a revolutionary scale. It says the early Lowell system was distinguished by state-of-the-art technology, its waterpower system, monumental mill architecture, rational city planning, a dependence on cotton grown by enslaved peoples and, most of all, its workforce of Yankee “mill girls.” As the factories aged, wages were cut and the mill girls gave way to immigrant workers; eight of the city’s ten original textile firms closed in the 1920s and the last two in the 1950s. [2]

In the late 1960s a federal Model Cities program proposed revitalizing the city through its heritage, a 1972 city council resolution adopted an “historical park concept,” and President Carter signed the law creating Lowell National Historical Park on June 5, 1978. [1] Its partner-driven management, the foundation document says, had no direct precedent in the national park system. Its boundary encloses 142 acres, only 19 of them federally owned, and almost all of downtown’s 5.3 million square feet of historic mill buildings have since been rehabilitated. [2]

indigenous.html: The undated park brochure describes the tribes of the Pennacook Confederacy meeting at Pawtucket Falls each spring to fish and settle tribal affairs. [1] The 2023 historic resource study by Stephanie Fortado and Emily Twarog uses the Western Abenaki name for the river, Molôdomek, rejecting the colonial picture of an empty land. It quotes Gregory Gray Fitzsimons’s estimate that “possibly as much as” 95 percent of the population perished after a 1616–19 plague and the 1633–34 smallpox pandemic. In 1653 the Massachusetts General Court seized land for Chelmsford and set aside about 1,500 acres along the rivers as Indian Territory; King Philip’s War (1675–76) followed, in which, by some counts, 5,000 people died, three-quarters of them Indigenous, and more than a thousand Native people were sold into slavery in the West Indies. In the 1680s Chelmsford settlers bought the Indian land. The Pennacook, the authors insist, did not simply vanish. [2]

labor_ccc.html: By 1845, the undated park brochure says, operatives were working longer hours under worsening conditions, turning out more cloth for less pay than when the mills opened. [1] In 1834 eight hundred women walked out over a 15 percent cut in piece rates, invoking ancestors who “preferred privation to bondage”; the 2023 study reads that language as reflecting a wider working-class wish to be distinguished from enslaved Black people. [2] The strike failed, but the brochure traces the Factory Girls Association of 1836 to it. Walkouts in 1853 cut the workday at Lowell and Lawrence from thirteen hours to eleven; a citywide strike failed in 1903, and in 1912 the Industrial Workers of the World won raises of six to eight percent. Irish laborers led by Hugh Cummiskey walked from Boston in 1822 to dig the canals, followed by French-Canadians, Greeks, Portuguese, Poles, Jews, Armenians, an African American community in the 1870s, and later Asian and Hispanic newcomers. [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Lowell National Historical Park archive page — overview (from an undated NPS brochure) and establishment block

slavery.html: Lowell’s cotton came from plantations worked by enslaved people. The foundation document names that dependence among the defining features of the Lowell system. [3] The 2023 historic resource study goes further: the Boston Associates made their fortunes in trade built on plantation goods, and Israel Thorndike and Nathan Appleton were growing wealthy from southern cotton fields before the Lowell mills began. It quotes historian Edward Baptist’s figure that from the 1830s Lowell’s mills used 5.5 million pounds of cleaned cotton a year, which “consumed 100,000 days of enslaved people’s labor every year,” and notes, following Baptist, that slaveholders also bought northern cloth for enslaved workers. Kirk Boott was vocally proslavery; in 1834 Lowell residents formed men’s and women’s antislavery societies, and historian Sean Griffin counts labor leader Sarah Bagley among reformers “unequivocal” against slavery. Baptist’s work, the authors conclude, makes it impossible to adequately tell Lowell’s history without the history of slavery. [4]

women.html: To run the mills, the Boston Associates recruited the daughters of Yankee farmers. Living in company boardinghouses under strict codes, women worked twelve-hour days, six days a week, to a bell, for $2.25 to $4.25 a week, minus $1.25 for room and board. They came to earn dowries, help the family farm, or become independent, and from 1840 to 1845 they edited and published the Lowell Offering, an early women’s literary magazine. [1] Sarah Bagley, born in 1806, praised factory work in an 1840 Offering essay; within a few years she had turned to founding the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association, taken over The Voice of Industry, and called the Offering’s editor “a mouthpiece of the corporations.” The 2023 historic resource study quotes Jocelyn Boryczka’s argument that Lowell’s rebellious mill women made revolutionary claims for women’s rights before the 1848 Seneca Falls declaration. [2]

MACA.summary:
Beneath the sandstone and shale ridges of Kentucky’s Edmonson, Hart and Barren counties lies the longest known cave system in the world: by 2014, the foundation document says, 400 miles had been surveyed (the park brochure gives over 365 miles), with underground rivers still carving new passages up to 450 feet below the surface. The cave holds one of the world’s most diverse cave ecosystems, and the Green River, running 27 miles through the park, is among the most biologically diverse rivers in North America. People have been drawn to this country for nearly 10,000 years. [1] [2]

Mammoth Cave was a tourist attraction by 1816, older than any national park. Its saltpetre was mined for gunpowder before and during the War of 1812, and the park’s 2023 historic resource study says enslaved people played a major role in making the cave a successful business. The park was authorized in 1926, a year after caver Floyd Collins’s death in Sand Cave drew national attention, and it was fully established in 1941; it now covers 53,000 surface acres and became a World Heritage Site in 1981. The brochure warns that park status does not guarantee protection: the cave’s groundwater begins far beyond the boundary and carries agricultural runoff, human waste, highway spills and drilling waste into the cave streams. [2] [3]

black.html:
After emancipation Black guides kept working the cave, and the Bransfords and their descendants guided there for over 100 years, while other Black workers were limited to jobs such as porter, cook and laundress. Tours were almost completely segregated. In 1921 Matt and Zemmie Bransford opened a 14-room summer resort on Flint Ridge for Black travelers; the Kentucky National Park Commission bought it for $3,000 in December 1934 to make way for the park. [1] [2]

A Black CCC company, camp NP-1, spent 12,000 man-days on cave improvements, completing 24 miles of trails. Yet by the end of 1939 every Black guide had been forced to retire, and when the Park Service took over the tours none were rehired, including Clifton, Arthur, Eddie, Elzie and George Bransford, leaving an all-white guide force for the first time since 1838. [2]

indigenous.html: Paleo-Indians hunted in the Green River valley more than 10,000 years ago. Between about 5,000 and 1,500 years ago, the park’s 2021 ethnographic overview reports, people ventured more than a mile into Mammoth and Salts caves to live, explore, mine minerals, hold ceremonies and bury their dead; the caves preserved their textiles, torch material and plant remains, some of the best evidence of early plant domestication in Kentucky, from sunflower and goosefoot to squash. The park brochure gives a narrower span, 4,000 to 2,000 years ago, and notes cane reed torches preserved in drier passageways. Seven federally recognized tribes claim the area as ancestral land: the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, Cherokee Nation, United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians, Absentee Shawnee Tribe, Eastern Shawnee Tribe, Shawnee Tribe and Chickasaw Nation. The overview notes the park has never systematically studied their oral histories of the place. [1] [2]

slavery.html:
From the early 1790s through the War of 1812, the park’s 2023 historic resource study reports, an estimated 70 enslaved workers, many leased from surrounding counties, dug and hauled nitrate-bearing dirt by torchlight and stood in leaching vats stirring it; the cave produced 300 to 500 pounds of saltpetre a day. [1]

Enslaved men also became its renowned guides. From 1838 Stephen Bishop, guiding at 17, and Mat and Nick Bransford, owned or leased by the cave’s owners, led tours that could last up to 18 hours. Bishop was the first to cross the Bottomless Pit and drew a map of the cave from memory, published in 1845. Owner John Croghan’s will valued Bishop at $600, his wife Charlotte at $450 and their son Thomas at $100, freeing them seven years after his death; they gained freedom in 1856, and Bishop died the next year. [2] [1]

MANA.name: Manassas National Battlefield Park
MANA.summary: Manassas National Battlefield Park in Prince William County, Virginia, preserves the site of two major Civil War battles. The First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) on July 21, 1861, was the war's first major land engagement, shattering both sides' expectations of a quick conflict and earning Confederate General Thomas J. Jackson his famous nickname "Stonewall." The Second Battle of Manassas, fought August 28–30, 1862, was a decisive Confederate victory that brought Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia to the doorstep of Washington, D.C. and set the stage for Lee's first invasion of the North. The battlefield was designated a national battlefield park in 1940 and preserves approximately 5,000 acres of the historic landscape.

MEMY.summary:
Shortly after midnight on June 12, 1963, Medgar Evers was shot in the carport of the house in Jackson, Mississippi, that he shared with his wife Myrlie and their three young children. The Park Service describes his death as the first murder of a nationally significant leader of the civil rights movement; it heightened public awareness of civil rights and became a catalyst for passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. [1]

The house itself records the danger the family lived with. Built in 1956, it stands in the Elraine Subdivision, the first post–World War II subdivision created for middle-class African Americans in Mississippi, developed by Black entrepreneur Winston J. Thompson with most houses built by Black builder Leroy Burnett. The couple turned down a corner lot they thought too exposed, chose a side entrance under the carport instead of a front door, and set furniture before the windows to block gunfire; Medgar taught the children to crawl infantry-style to the bathroom if they heard strange noises. The house also served as an extension of the NAACP office, where the couple hosted civil rights workers and sheltered African Americans threatened by white supremacists. [1] [1]

Myrlie Evers moved to California in 1964, rented the house out for thirty years and donated it in 1993 to Tougaloo College, which has operated it as a museum. It was designated a National Historic Landmark on December 23, 2016, authorized as a national monument on March 12, 2019, and established as a unit of the National Park System on November 9, 2020. The park’s foundation document calls the violation of the home a solemn reminder of the danger of unchecked racism and discrimination, which it says the country still struggles to eradicate. [1] [1] [1]

black.html:
Medgar Evers, born in Decatur in 1925, served in segregated Army units in Europe during World War II. Refused admission to the University of Mississippi law school in 1954, he became the NAACP’s first field secretary in Mississippi, its first salaried post in the state, in January 1955, according to the landmark nomination; the foundation document gives 1954. He investigated racially motivated killings — in 1955 alone those of Emmett Till, the Rev. George Lee and Lamar Smith — took reporters to the crime scenes, and helped James Meredith enter the University of Mississippi in 1962. [1] [1] [1]

On May 28, 1963, a Molotov cocktail was thrown onto the carport. On June 12 a sniper fired from about 200 feet away. Byron De La Beckwith, whom the park describes as a white supremacist and a member of the segregationist White Citizens’ Council, was tried twice in 1964 before all-white, all-male juries that deadlocked; he was convicted of murder in 1994. [1] [1]

women.html: The foundation document calls Medgar and Myrlie Evers committed and equal partners. Myrlie served as his secretary during his first two years as field secretary, then chose to stay home, where much of her time went to hosting civil rights leaders, often overnight, and sheltering Black victims of abuse and threats. After the assassination she became a national speaker for the NAACP, received its Spingarn Medal in July 1963 and testified at both of Beckwith’s 1964 trials. In California she earned a sociology degree from Pomona College in 1968, became the first African American woman on the Los Angeles Board of Public Works, chaired the NAACP board from 1995 to 1998, and in 2013 became the first woman to deliver a presidential inaugural invocation. [1] [1]

MONO.name: Monocacy National Battlefield
MONO.summary: Monocacy National Battlefield near Frederick, Maryland, preserves the site of the Battle of Monocacy, fought on July 9, 1864 — often called "The Battle That Saved Washington." When Confederate General Jubal Early led an army toward the Union capital, a hastily assembled force of Union soldiers under General Lew Wallace (later the author of "Ben-Hur") delayed Early's advance for an entire day at the Monocacy River crossing. Although the Union forces were defeated, the delay allowed reinforcements to reach Washington's defenses in time to prevent the capital's capture. The battlefield was established as a national battlefield in 1934 and preserves 1,647 acres of agricultural landscape and historic structures.

MORA.summary:
Mount Rainier is the tallest volcano in the Cascade Range and the most heavily glaciated peak in the continental United States, a 14,410-foot mountain whose rivers of ice run up to 750 feet deep while steam still escapes from vents at its summit. Below the ice the seasons are compressed: in the subalpine meadows summer may last only two months, and the wildflowers, insects, birds and mammals race through it before the snow returns. [1]

Archaeological findings suggest people have been coming to the mountain for more than 9,000 years. Congress made it the nation’s fifth national park on March 2, 1899, and in 1988 designated more than 97 percent of it as wilderness. Nearly two million people a year now walk its meadows and old-growth forest and sleep in rustic log-and-boulder lodges built a century ago, in a landscape the Park Service itself calls anything but permanent: ice and rock break away from the peak, rivers of meltwater and debris wreak havoc with roads and buildings, and the brochure handed to visitors concedes that as the planet warms, no one knows how the mountain’s plants, animals or visitors will fare. [1]

climate.html: The Nisqually Glacier, visible from the road to Paradise, has been watched longer than almost any glacier in America: its terminus was first recorded in 1857, and it has since retreated more than two and a quarter kilometres up the mountain. Weather stations at Longmire and Paradise show the forty-five years from 1970 to 2015 growing 1.5 °C warmer and 0.77 metres drier, and the glacier losing another 280 metres of length in that span; researchers expect it to keep shrinking unless the climate changes. The ice does not go quietly. Ten outburst floods have surged from the glacier in the period of record, nine of them during retreat, sending water and rock down the Nisqually toward the park’s roads and buildings. [4] [5]

indigenous.html:
Long before it was a park, the mountain was a late-summer destination. The ethnographer Allan H. Smith, whose 1960s fieldwork Catton reports (and partly questions), identified five peoples who used it — the Nisqually, Puyallup, Muckleshoot, Yakima (today’s Yakama Nation) and Taidnapam: families climbed from the lowland valleys and over the passes to camp in the high meadows when the huckleberries ripened, to hunt deer, elk and mountain goat, and occasionally to seek spirit power. Each fall they set fire to the meadows so the berry patches would spread — a practice park officials never understood and never continued. Early accounts rendered the mountain’s name as “Takhoma,” though Catton cautions that much of what settlers wrote about Indian belief was shaped to suit their own purposes. [2] [3]

The treaties of 1854 and 1855 that ceded this country reserved the privilege of hunting and gathering roots and berries on “open and unclaimed land,” but after 1899 park officials treated the mountain as closed. In 1915 the Interior Department’s solicitor concluded that the treaty right had survived the park’s creation; a year later the Park Service’s chief clerk advised that state law and two court decisions had superseded that opinion, and rangers kept enforcing the ban. In October 1917 six Yakima people — four men and two women, by the newspaper account Catton quotes — were arrested at Yakima Park with freshly skinned deer hides and fined. Catton’s conclusion is that the park amplified and distorted Indian legends at the same time as it altered Indian use of the mountain. Descendants of those nations still hold the mountain as a place of special connection today. [2] [1]

labor_ccc.html: Much of what visitors still touch at Rainier — the stone guardrails, log cabins and campgrounds — was built by young men of the Depression. By mid-July 1933 more than a thousand Civilian Conservation Corps enrollees, single men aged 18 to 25 from families on relief, were at work in five park camps; many companies were shipped west by train, including three from New York and one from Illinois in the first season and, in 1937, a company of 140 from Arkansas. One crew spent 703 man-days on a single mile of trail past Narada Falls. The Corps was segregated nationally: Black enrollees were underrepresented and mostly formed into separate companies, and Native Americans were enrolled in a separate Indian Division that worked on reservations. Public Works Administration money nominally outspent the CCC, CWA and WPA combined at Rainier — a figure Catton calls deceiving, since much of it continued the 1920s road program — but it is the Corps’ log cabins, stone comfort stations and stone guardrails that Catton calls its most enduring legacy. [7]

sources.title: Catton, Wonderland (1996), ch. 11, The Impact of the New Deal

women.html: On the afternoon of August 10, 1890, Fay Fuller, a nineteen-year-old Tacoma schoolteacher, stood on the summit in ankle-length bloomers after a two-day climb with four men — the first woman known to have reached the top. Three summers earlier a party had let her come along only on condition that she turn back at 8,500 feet; she went home resolved to go as high as she could. Guide Leonard Longmire, remembering her in 1933, said she rode astride rather than sidesaddle and drilled with rifles alongside a group of young Tacoma women who called themselves the Women’s Guard — behaviour, Potts suggests, that drew criticism from townspeople. Her published account drew fresh attention to the mountain and to mountaineering, particularly for women. [6]

MORR.name: Morristown National Historical Park
MORR.summary: Morristown National Historical Park in Morristown, New Jersey, was the first national historical park in the United States, established on March 2, 1933. The park preserves sites associated with two critical winter encampments of the Continental Army during the American Revolution. During the winter of 1779–1780, General George Washington quartered his army of approximately 10,000 soldiers at Jockey Hollow, where they endured what was recorded as the coldest winter of the 18th century — with 28 snowstorms and temperatures colder than at Valley Forge. Washington used the nearby Ford Mansion as his headquarters. The park also preserves Fort Nonsense and the New Jersey Brigade encampment area.

MORU.summary:
Mount Rushmore is a 5,725-foot granite peak in the Black Hills of South Dakota, rising in a nearly circular shape within the semi-arid Northern Plains as an oasis of vegetation among dry grasslands. The Lakota call the range Paha Sapa or He Sapa, rendered in English as “hills that are black,” and the mountain itself Tunkasila Sakpe Paha, Six Grandfathers Mountain, or Igmu Tanka Paha, Cougar Mountain. [1] Into its southeast-facing granite wall sculptor Gutzon Borglum’s crews carved George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln and Theodore Roosevelt — fourteen years of work, only six of them spent on actual carving, until the work stopped in October 1941. [1]

The idea began as a way to draw sightseers: in 1923 state historian Doane Robinson suggested carving giant statues in the Black Hills, and the backers then called in the sculptor who was carving a Confederate memorial on Stone Mountain in Georgia. Federal money supplied $836,000 of a total cost of nearly $1 million. [1] The 2016 Historic Resource Study notes that Borglum “joined the Klan briefly, to secure financial backing from its prominent members” for the Stone Mountain project. [1] The 2015 foundation document dates the memorial’s enabling law to March 3, 1925; NPSHistory gives its establishment as February 25, 1929, the date of the act that also forbids any admission charge. [1] [1]

The memorial came under National Park Service stewardship in 1933. Its 1,278 acres hold old-growth ponderosa pine, granite peaks, historic buildings and archeological sites, and visitation has reached over three million people in recent years. The foundation document calls the Black Hills sacred spaces for living cultures, and among its interpretive themes states that the memorial “reveals the contrast of cultural ideals and the reality of the American experience.” [1]

indigenous.html:
Crow, Kiowa, Kiowa-Apache, Cheyenne and Lakota peoples all used the Black Hills over several hundred years before U.S. expansion, and Lakota call the Paha Sapa wamakaognaka e’cante, “the heart of everything that is.” The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie placed the Hills inside Lakota territory and required three-fourths of adult men to approve any change. After Custer’s 1874 expedition reported gold, President Grant ordered in November 1875 that the army stop resisting miners entering the Hills. Congress in 1877 ratified an agreement signed by only ten percent of adult men. [1]

In 1980 the Supreme Court upheld the Lakota claim that the Hills had been taken without just compensation, but the Lakota have refused payment; the Oglala Tribal Council at Pine Ridge had resolved in 1978 that “the Black Hills are not for sale.” In August 1970 twenty-three American Indians climbed Mount Rushmore to protest the taking. [1] The memorial consults today with 21 associated tribal nations. [1]

sources.title: Reed & Wallace, Shrine of Democracy and Sacred Stone: Historic Resource Study, Mount Rushmore National Memorial (NPS, 2016)

labor_ccc.html: Between 350 and 400 people worked on the mountain over the fourteen years of construction, by the Historic Resource Study’s count (the foundation document says more than 400 local workers). Many came from the Keystone area with experience in the gold and feldspar mines or in logging. A common laborer earned $.40 an hour in 1927–28 and $.50 from 1929, but only $.35 in 1932, when wages were paid through a federal relief program. The study calls Borglum’s “bosun chair” harnesses quite safe and records no major accidents and no deaths at Rushmore, but stone dust left many with silicosis, and James Champion, Eldon Gordon, Hoot Leach and Earl Oaks died of it. Two 200-man Civilian Conservation Corps camps stood at nearby Custer State Park, but Borglum opposed using the Corps and its role at Rushmore was limited; CCC crews did lay the stone steps and walkway between his studio and the Borglum View Terrace. [1] [1]

women.html: The carving was largely a man’s domain, but the Historic Resource Study identifies fifteen women who worked at Rushmore, most of them workers’ wives. Carol Swenson was hired at sixteen to operate the gift/information center in the first sculptor’s studio, counting visitors and ordering supplies for four or five summers around her 1933 graduation. Her sister Gladys Swenson Hallsted ran the bunkhouse and dining room with her husband, serving 35-cent meals. Mary Cerasani led tourists to the top of the mountain in 1940. Maxine Wasser was Clerk of the Works from 1935 through 1938, and Jean Philip, whose mother was of American Indian descent, handled correspondence and payroll as assistant office manager from 1938 through 1941. [1]

MUWO.name: Muir Woods National Monument
MUWO.summary: Muir Woods National Monument in Marin County, California, protects 554 acres of old-growth coast redwood forest in a sheltered valley on the Pacific coast just north of San Francisco. The monument was established by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 after Congressman William Kent and his wife Elizabeth Thacher Kent purchased the land to save it from logging and donated it to the federal government. Kent requested that the monument be named in honor of naturalist John Muir, who called it "the best tree-lovers monument that could possibly be found in all the forests of the world." Some of the redwood trees in the monument are over 250 feet tall and more than 1,000 years old. The monument is part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site component in the Redwood National and State Parks serial nomination.

NAMA.summary:
For more than two centuries the National Mall — the great green swath that runs from the foot of the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River — has been the nation’s premier civic and symbolic space. National Mall and Memorial Parks cares for it and more than 1,000 acres of parkland across Washington: the Washington Monument and the Lincoln, Jefferson, Roosevelt, King, Korean War, Vietnam Veterans, World War I and World War II memorials, Ford’s Theatre, Pennsylvania Avenue, and more than 150 circles, squares and small reservations, from the African American Civil War Memorial to Logan Circle. [1] [2]

Its open spaces are as old as the capital: Pierre L’Enfant’s 1791 plan, commissioned by President Washington, laid them out as a stage for remembrance, celebration and the exercise of First Amendment rights, and federal review bodies are still charged with protecting both it and the 1901 McMillan Plan. For decades the federal government largely neglected the Mall itself; after its oak forest was cleared in the 1810s it became eroded scrubland where pigs and cows grazed. The parks passed to the National Park Service in 1933, and today they draw more than 33 million visitors a year to a place that, in the Park Service’s words, hosts history in the making — from presidential inaugurals to civil rights demonstrations. [2] [3]

black.html: In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let the African American opera singer Marian Anderson sing at Constitution Hall, which kept a White-performers-only policy; the segregated D.C. school board also turned her away. Organizers turned instead to the Lincoln Memorial, and Interior Secretary Harold Ickes, whose Park Service managed it, handled most of the arrangements. On Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, Anderson sang from the memorial’s steps to an integrated crowd of 75,000 that stretched toward the Washington Monument. The study quotes historian Scott Sandage’s judgment that with the concert the civil rights movement began to develop a strategy of mass, symbolic protest. On August 28, 1963, more than 200,000 people marched from the Washington Monument to the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom; Anderson opened it with the national anthem, and Martin Luther King Jr. delivered “I Have a Dream.” [3]

sources.title: Events and Celebrations on the National Mall HRS (NPS, 2024), ch. 'The Making of a Political and Protest Space (1930–1963)', PDF pp. 208–219

climate.html: Part of the park sits on ground taken from the river: West and East Potomac parks were built on reclaimed land, and the 2017 foundation document reports that the seawalls built to keep the water out are crumbling and failing. Both parks remain vulnerable to river flooding and sea level rise even with portions of the Potomac Park levee completed; the park’s own headquarters lay below the normal high tide line, where high water had become a regular occurrence, and the area around the Tidal Basin is a major concern. The document expects the problem to be made worse by climate change’s effects on sea level and storm surges, and calls it a critical issue for the park. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, National Mall and Memorial Parks (2017) — Key Issues: Climate Change, Environmental Impacts, and Sea Level Rise, PDF p. 37

slavery.html: In the early nineteenth century, the 2024 historic resource study notes, the horror of American slavery was on full display on the Mall: pens holding enslaved people stood at its edge at 7th Street NW, and coffles of enslaved men and women, chained together, were marched across it to the loading docks on the Potomac. [3] North of the Mall, at Vermont Avenue and U Street NW, the African American Civil War Memorial honors the more than 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors who served in the U.S. Army and Navy during the Civil War — service that, the foundation document says, helped end the war and free more than four million enslaved people. The memorial’s curved walls carry the names of the men who served. [2]

women.html: On March 3, 1913, the day before Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration, the National American Woman Suffrage Association’s Woman Suffrage Procession, organized by Alice Paul and Lucy Burns, marched down Pennsylvania Avenue from the Capitol toward the Treasury. A crowd of about 250,000 spilled into the street; men heckled, spat on and assaulted the marchers while police proved unable or unwilling to control them. The protests kept coming. Paul and Burns joined Alva Belmont in founding the National Woman’s Party in 1916, and through 1917 more than 1,000 women picketed the White House; between June and November police arrested 218 of them for “obstructing sidewalk traffic.” Wilson signaled support for the suffrage amendment in January 1918, and the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. The Park Service’s 2024 study credits the 1913 march with further establishing Washington as a national stage for large-scale demonstration. [3]

NATR.summary:
The Natchez Trace Parkway runs 444 miles through Mississippi, Alabama and Tennessee, from the bluffs of the lower Mississippi River at Natchez to the Appalachian foothills near Nashville, along a corridor whose human use the Park Service dates to 8000 BCE. It began, the 2014 foundation document says, as animal trails, and became a human route because it followed high ground and easily passable topography; 180 segments of the original route survive, some worn into a sunken profile where foot, horse and wagon traffic cut into erodible loess soil. The corridor crosses the homelands of the Natchez, Chickasaw and Choctaw nations, links more than 350 archeological sites and 22 burial and ceremonial mounds, and protects more than 2,600 species across seven ecoregions. [1] [2]

By 1785 the Trace was a route for boatmen who floated down the Mississippi to sell their goods in Natchez and New Orleans. President Thomas Jefferson designated it a national post road in 1801, Meriwether Lewis died on it in 1809, and General Andrew Jackson moved militia and regular troops along it during the War of 1812. Stands, or inns, provided lodging, food and drink to travelers. Congress created the parkway in 1938 to commemorate the route; it took from a groundbreaking on September 16, 1937, to May 21, 2005, to finish. [1] [2] [3]

One of the foundation document’s interpretive themes, “Homelands in Transition,” holds that generations of American Indian occupation came to an end as Americans migrated westward; four sections of the Trail of Tears and parts of the Choctaw and Chickasaw removal routes cross the parkway. The document also records that interpretation had not focused on the message that mound sites are sacred, and that climate models predict heavier rainfall that could accelerate erosion and expose buried cultural resources along the corridor. [1]

indigenous.html:
A 1994 National Register nomination describes the Trace as interlocking Native paths running from the Cumberland settlements to the Chickasaw villages, on to the Choctaw towns, and from there to the villages of the Natchez on the Mississippi. Emerald Mound, an eight-acre ceremonial mound built between 1200 and 1730, is the nation’s second-largest, according to the foundation document. [1] [2] [3]

At milepost 397.4 the Old Trace marks the boundary of Chickasaw lands ceded to the United States in 1805 and 1816. In 1811 Choctaw agent Silas Dinsmoor moved his agency to a site beside the road; travelers passing through the Choctaw Nation had to display a pass to him. In the 1820 Treaty of Doaks Stand the Choctaws gave up six million acres and agreed to move west; it took another ten years and a second treaty before they went. More than 20 tribes have an ancestral connection to the Trace and hold its mounds as sacred ground. [2] [1] [3]

slavery.html:
Mount Locust, at milepost 15.5, was a cotton plantation as well as a stand; the Park Service’s 2022 draft landscape inventory states that it ran on enslaved labor until after the Civil War. It counts 26 enslaved workers in Paulina Ferguson’s household in the 1820 census, 42 in 1830, and 53 in her 1849 estate appraisal, divided among her three surviving children. The 1860 Jefferson County slave census shows T. Chamberlain with 72 enslaved workers and 16 enslaved houses. Mount Locust’s slave dwellings have not been found; 1998 archeology mapped 42 regularly shaped depressions in their cemetery, on a wooded ridge northwest of the house; burials appear arranged by families. [1]

In late 1811 Andrew Jackson, travelling to Natchez to obtain enslaved people, refused to show his pass at the Choctaw Agency and armed several of the enslaved people with him; agent Dinsmoor, himself an enslaver on the agency land, armed Indians and whites. No blood was shed. [1]

women.html:
Elizabeth Female Academy, at Washington, Mississippi, six miles east of Natchez, was chartered on February 17, 1818, on grounds that Elizabeth Roach donated to the Methodist Mississippi Conference, and opened on November 12 that year. Bishop Charles Galloway, writing in 1899, called it the first chartered institution for the higher education of young women in the South, if not in the United States; the park brochure calls it the first school for women chartered by Mississippi. It did collegiate work and conferred degrees, took 28 to 63 boarders a year between 1819 and 1829, and counted John James Audubon on its faculty. The capital’s move to Jackson, yellow fever epidemics and other causes forced it to suspend operation in 1845; by 1974 one brick wall stood. [1] [2]

Up the road at Mount Locust, family tradition holds that Paulina Ferguson divorced James Chamberlain in 1816 and ran the house as a stand until around 1842. [3]

NRSS.name: Natural Resource Stewardship
NRSS.summary: The National Park Service's natural resource stewardship mission dates to the agency's founding in 1916, when the Organic Act charged the NPS with conserving "the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein" for the enjoyment of future generations. The NPS Natural Resource Stewardship and Science Directorate oversees programs in biological resources, geologic resources, water resources, air quality, climate change science, and inventory and monitoring across more than 400 park units. These scientific programs produce peer-reviewed research that informs park management decisions and contributes to the broader scientific understanding of ecosystem health, biodiversity, and environmental change across the nation's most protected landscapes.

ORPI.name: Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument
ORPI.summary: Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in southwestern Arizona protects 330,689 acres of Sonoran Desert wilderness along the U.S.–Mexico border — the only place in the United States where the organ pipe cactus grows wild. Proclaimed a national monument in 1937, the park was designated a UNESCO International Biosphere Reserve in 1976 in recognition of its outstanding desert ecosystem biodiversity. The monument harbors 28 species of cactus, over 270 species of birds, and rare mammals including the Sonoran pronghorn, one of the most endangered land mammals in North America. The Tohono O'odham people have lived in and around the monument's lands for centuries and maintain cultural connections to the landscape. The monument's location on the international border has made it a focal point in immigration and border security debates.

PAIS.summary:
A few miles off the south Texas coast, Padre Island National Seashore protects what its 2015 brochure calls the world’s longest undeveloped stretch of barrier island: 70 miles of sand-and-shell beaches, wind-sculpted dunes, grasslands and tidal flats between the Gulf and the Laguna Madre, one of only six hypersaline lagoons in the world. Wind, waves and storms keep reshaping it, and the whole island is slowly moving toward the mainland. Around 380 bird species — almost 45 percent of those in North America — have been recorded here, and it is the nation’s prime nesting beach for the endangered Kemp’s ridley sea turtle. [1]

People used the island long before Europeans: the park’s 2016 foundation document dates its cultural resources first to the Karankawa, who used it for food and refuge, and says Spanish troops bound for Mexico and shipwreck victims visited only infrequently from Spanish discovery into the early 19th century. [2] The 1999 administrative history records an ill-fated 1554 Spanish expedition and says the Balli family — a priest and his nephew who received a Spanish grant — began ranching the island and gave it its name; from 1879 Patrick Dunn, the “Duke of Padre,” ranched here into the 1920s. [3] The foundation document says ranching lasted until 1970 and that the park also holds a Mexican-American War campsite and artifacts from the island’s World War II use as a bombing area. [2]

After Senator Ralph Yarborough introduced the first park bill in 1958, Congress passed the seashore bill and President John F. Kennedy signed it on September 28, 1962. [3] Lady Bird Johnson dedicated the park on April 8, 1968. [4]

climate.html: The 2016 foundation document warns that rising seas, more frequent or intense storms and more extreme heat projected for the region could damage sea turtle nests and eggs, shift hatchling sex ratios, and disrupt oxygen exchange in eggs through saltwater intrusion. [2] A 2017 Park Service vulnerability assessment of 43 structures and 44 roads, parking lots and other transportation assets, looking ahead to 2050, found most assets had low or moderate exposure, in part because of relatively high elevations and an accreting shoreline — yet 38 percent were highly vulnerable to coastal hazards and sea-level rise, including 61 percent of transportation assets; the most valuable among them include sections of Park Road, the Bird Island Basin waterfront and the Malaquite visitor center parking. Those highly vulnerable assets were worth about $64.5 million, roughly three-quarters of the value assessed. [10]

indigenous.html: The park’s website (last updated 2021) estimates the island formed 3,000 to 5,000 years ago and says Native American points found here indicate it has probably been visited, if not inhabited, since it formed. The peoples who most recently inhabited the South Texas coast, it says, were the Karankawa, who ranged between Corpus Christi Bay and Galveston, and Coahuiltecan bands ranging south into Mexico, among them the Malaquites, for whom Malaquite Beach is named. [5] The park’s 1971 historic resource study reports about 20 Karankawa campsites found in the island’s first twenty miles, visited seasonally and probably in summer. [6] The 1999 administrative history says the Karankawa survived well into the nineteenth century [7]; the 2021 web page says they “existed as a people in Texas until about 1850.” [5] The 2016 foundation document lists seven traditionally associated tribes: the Alabama-Coushatta, Apache Tribe of Oklahoma, Comanche, Fort Sill Apache, Kiowa, Mescalero Apache and Tonkawa. [2]

women.html: At a Senate subcommittee hearing on the seashore bill, Esther Goodrich of the Texas Conservation Council argued for a larger seashore with a roadless center, warning that parks once thought ample for generations were already crowded. [8] In 1986 biological technician Donna Shaver took charge of the park’s sea turtle work; that year, under her guidance, staff and volunteers began beach patrols for nesting turtles, and in May 1996 she and others documented the first return of a head-started Kemp’s ridley to the seashore, a turtle from the 1987 class that laid 83 eggs. Her incubation research helped raise the park’s hatch success to 90 percent and was shared with scientists at Rancho Nuevo, Mexico. The 1999 administrative history says the Kemp’s ridley project “may be considered” one of the park administration’s most successful natural resource programs. [9]

PETE.name: Petersburg National Battlefield
PETE.summary: Petersburg National Battlefield in Virginia preserves the sites associated with the Siege of Petersburg, a nine-month campaign from June 1864 to April 1865 that ultimately led to the end of the Civil War. General Ulysses S. Grant's strategy to cut the vital railroad supply lines feeding the Confederate capital at Richmond resulted in one of the war's longest sustained operations, with miles of trenches foreshadowing the trench warfare of World War I. The siege included the Battle of the Crater on July 30, 1864, in which Union forces detonated a mine beneath Confederate lines — an assault that ended in a disastrous Union defeat and particularly heavy casualties among United States Colored Troops. The fall of Petersburg on April 2, 1865, led directly to the evacuation of Richmond and Lee's surrender at Appomattox a week later.

PIRO.summary:
Sandstone cliffs streaked ochre, tan and brown, with bands of white and green, rise 50 to 200 feet out of Lake Superior along the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. The colors come from groundwater seeping through cracks and leaving iron, manganese, copper and other minerals on the rock face; the cliffs themselves are largely 500-million-year-old Cambrian sandstone under a harder cap rock, carved by the lake into arches. The last glacier, which began retreating about 10,000 years ago, left kettle lakes and wetlands, and created the four-square-mile perched dune of the Grand Sable Banks. [1] [1]

People have come here since the ice withdrew. Archaic and Woodland peoples made summer camps along the coast, and later Anishinaabe people (the brochure’s Anishinaabek) hunted and fished here, as their descendants still do. The French fur trader Pierre Esprit Radisson, the first documented visitor to the Pictured Rocks, passed in 1658 and called the coast most delightful and wonderful. In the late 1800s boomtowns on the south shore supported large logging operations and blast furnaces making pig iron for the railroads, and the Life-Saving Service and Lighthouse Service built stations to help ships past the treacherous rock reef. [1] [1]

On October 15, 1966, President Lyndon Johnson signed the law creating the first national lakeshore here. It hugs more than 40 miles of shoreline, and with its Inland Buffer Zone of federal, state and private land covers nearly 73,000 acres. Historian Theodore Karamanski argues that the buffer zone and scenic drive were the law’s most controversial features, born of a consensus that masked deep divisions and later sharpened bitterness between local people and the Park Service. [1] [1]

indigenous.html:
This shore was part of the land of the Ojibwe (Ojibwa in Karamanski’s 1995 administrative history). In 1658 Radisson’s Indian companions called the cliffs Nauitouchsinagoit, which he took to mean “the likeness of the devil,” and left an offering of tobacco there; Karamanski reads this as consistent with Ojibwe belief in a world alive with spirits. The Grand Sable Dunes, Negouwatchi or the Sandy Mountain, also received tobacco from Ojibwe travelers. Karamanski judges that the lakeshore itself was not heavily used for living or subsistence, but that it served as a place of burial, at Sand Point and the Grand Sable Dunes, and is frequently mentioned in Ojibwe lore. [1]

The park’s 2016 foundation document calls Chapel, Little Beaver and Beaver lakes, the high cliffs, promontories and creek mouths of its wilderness study area especially important to the Ojibwe of the region, and notes that traditional ceremonies and plant gathering take place infrequently, mostly off-season. [1]

REER.name: Reconstruction Era Historical Park (National Monument)
REER.summary: Reconstruction Era National Historical Park in Beaufort County, South Carolina, was established in 2017 as the first unit of the National Park System dedicated to the Reconstruction era (1861–1900). The park preserves sites in and around Beaufort associated with the transition from slavery to freedom, including the Brick Baptist Church — where formerly enslaved people first learned to read — and the Darrah Hall at Penn Center, one of the first schools for freed African Americans in the South. The Sea Islands of South Carolina were among the earliest places where the federal government experimented with programs for formerly enslaved people, including land redistribution, education, and political participation. The park tells the stories of newly freed people who built schools, churches, and communities and exercised their rights as citizens during this transformative period.

RIRA.name: River Raisin National Battlefield Park
RIRA.summary: River Raisin National Battlefield Park in Monroe, Michigan, preserves the site of the January 1813 battles that were among the deadliest engagements of the War of 1812 on American soil. On January 22, 1813, a combined British and Native American force defeated a larger American army along the River Raisin, and the following day, wounded American prisoners were killed in what became known as the River Raisin Massacre — the deadliest single event for U.S. forces in the war. The rallying cry "Remember the Raisin!" became a powerful recruiting tool for the American war effort. The park was designated a national battlefield park in 2010, making it the 392nd unit of the National Park System and the only national battlefield park dedicated to the War of 1812.

ROCR.name: Rock Creek Park
ROCR.summary: Rock Creek Park in Washington, D.C., is one of the largest and oldest urban parks in the United States. Established by an act of Congress in 1890 — just two years after Yellowstone — the park preserves nearly 1,800 acres of forested valley along Rock Creek and its tributaries in the heart of the nation's capital. The park was created to protect the creek's watershed and provide a natural retreat for city residents during the rapid urbanization of late 19th-century Washington. Rock Creek Park includes the Civil War-era Fort DeRussy, Peirce Mill (a 19th-century grist mill), and significant archaeological sites with evidence of Native American habitation dating back thousands of years. The park's forests, trails, and Nature Center make it a vital green space in one of the country's most densely developed metropolitan areas.

SAAN.name: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park
SAAN.summary: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park in San Antonio, Texas, preserves four of the five Spanish colonial missions established along the San Antonio River in the 18th century: Mission Concepción, Mission San José, Mission San Juan, and Mission Espada. Together with the Alamo (Mission San Antonio de Valero), these missions represent the largest concentration of Spanish colonial missions in North America. Founded between 1718 and 1731 by Franciscan friars, the missions served as centers for converting and acculturating Native American peoples into Spanish colonial society. The park was established in 1978 and the missions were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 — the first World Heritage Site in Texas — recognized for their outstanding example of the interchange of Spanish and Coahuiltecan cultures.

SAJH.name: San Juan Island National Historical Park
SAJH.summary: San Juan Island National Historical Park in Washington State preserves the sites of the 1859 Pig War confrontation between the United States and Great Britain over possession of the San Juan Islands. The dispute began when an American settler shot a British-owned pig and escalated into a military standoff with both nations deploying forces on the island. The conflict was resolved through 12 years of joint military occupation and ultimately settled by international arbitration in 1872, when Kaiser Wilhelm I of Germany ruled in favor of the United States. The park preserves both the American Camp and English Camp — the respective military installations — and the island's prairie, forest, and shoreline ecosystems. The park was established in 1966.

SAJU.summary:
San Juan National Historic Site protects the stone defenses of San Juan Bay: Castillo San Felipe del Morro on the cliffs above the harbor entrance, Castillo San Cristóbal to the east, El Cañuelo across the bay on Isla de Cabras, and most of what remains of the wall around Old San Juan — in the foundation document’s words, the oldest and largest Spanish fortification system in the United States. [1] Trade winds and ocean currents carried sailing ships here from Europe, and Puerto Rico was the first major island with water, shelter and supplies on that route. Over ten generations and 250 years Spain built a system of defense in depth to guard its access to the wealth of the Americas: El Morro grew from a promontory with cannon into a six-level fortress, and Castillo San Cristóbal, built over 150 years against attack by land, is called by the park brochure the biggest European fortification in the Americas. [1]

The brochure’s timeline records English attacks on San Juan in 1595 and 1598, a Dutch attack in 1625 and a British attack in 1797. After the Spanish-American War, the 1898 Treaty of Paris transferred the forts and 210.86 acres to the U.S. military, which named the post Fort Brooke in 1943. In 1949 the Secretary of the Interior designated part of it a national historic site — on February 24, according to the foundation document; NPSHistory’s establishment list gives February 14. In 1983 UNESCO named it, with La Fortaleza, a World Heritage Site. [1] [1]

The park’s 75 acres are the largest open green space in Old San Juan. Its masons, trained in traditional techniques, preserve the stone fortifications, and the foundation document expects rising seas and stronger storm surges to contribute to the ongoing weathering of its centuries-old structures in a coastal environment. [1]

indigenous.html: Before European colonization the island was home to the Taíno, who called it Boriquén; Columbus and Juan Ponce de León stopped in 1493 and Columbus named it San Juan Bautista, the 2021 National Register documentation records. [1] Under Ponce de León, who began the colony in 1508, Spain displaced the Taíno, and the park brochure’s timeline marks a Taíno revolt in 1511. [1] The first stone fort, La Fortaleza (1533–1539), faced chiefly landward; the Register documentation reads that orientation as protection against attacks from the Taíno and from Carib people raiding from the Lesser Antilles. It also names Native Taíno among the peoples — with African, Spanish, Italian, Irish, English and others — who contributed to the design and construction of the fortifications themselves. [1]

latino.html: The 2021 National Register documentation finds the forts significant as a symbol of Puerto Rican identity. Under U.S. rule, it explains, Spanish architecture took on new meaning: elites disenfranchised by American colonial policy turned to the island’s Hispanic legacy, and the independence movement increasingly looked to the Spanish past. In 1912, when rat-infested walls were blamed for an outbreak of bubonic plague and the Army still declined to repair them, Governor George R. Colton urged that walls not needed for defense pass to the “People of Puerto Rico.” In 1926–27 engineer Martín Paniagua and the newspaper El Mundo attacked Army Corps of Engineers repairs in Portland cement, and the contractors agreed to reface the concrete with coral blocks. [1] The foundation document calls the site a potent symbol of cultural heritage linking Puerto Rico’s history to Hispanic culture and providing a common identity with other Latin American countries. [1]

SAND.name: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site
SAND.summary: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site in southeastern Colorado preserves the location where, on November 29, 1864, approximately 675 U.S. volunteer soldiers attacked a peaceful encampment of Cheyenne and Arapaho people, killing an estimated 150 to 200 men, women, children, and elders. The village, led by Chiefs Black Kettle and Left Hand, had been assured of safety by U.S. military officials, and an American flag and a white flag of surrender flew over the camp during the attack. The massacre was condemned by some contemporaries, including a Congressional investigation, but no perpetrators were prosecuted. The site was designated a national historic site in 2007 after extensive consultation with descendants of the Cheyenne and Arapaho victims, who participated in identifying the massacre location.

SARI.name: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve
SARI.summary: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve on the island of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands is the only known site where members of a Columbus expedition set foot on what is now U.S. territory. On November 14, 1493, during Columbus's second voyage, a landing party encountered the Kalinago (Carib) people in Salt River Bay — the encounter turned violent and is considered the first documented armed conflict between Europeans and Native Americans. The site also preserves a ceremonial ball court and village site of the Taino people, who inhabited the island before European contact. Established as a national historical park in 1992, Salt River Bay protects one of the largest remaining mangrove forests in the Virgin Islands and a rich marine ecosystem including coral reefs, seagrass beds, and a submarine canyon.

SCBL.name: Scotts Bluff National Monument
SCBL.summary: Scotts Bluff National Monument in western Nebraska preserves a prominent natural landmark along the North Platte River that served as a major waypoint on the Oregon Trail, California Trail, and Mormon Trail during the great westward migrations of the 19th century. The bluff, rising 800 feet above the river valley, was visible for miles and marked the passage through a gap in the series of steep bluffs that forced travelers to find specific routes through the terrain. An estimated 250,000 emigrants passed through Mitchell Pass at the base of the bluff between the 1840s and 1860s, and deep wagon wheel ruts are still visible today. The monument was established in 1919 and includes a museum with one of the finest collections of watercolors by pioneer artist William Henry Jackson.
